section: 1. Definition of Insurance Contract
stem: X pays Y P10,000 so that Y will pay X P1M if a named ship, already lost at sea but unknown to both, failed to arrive. Is this a valid subject of insurance?
answer: Yes, the undertaking is a valid subject of insurance because both parties were ignorant of the loss when the contract was perfected. Section 3 covers past contingent events unknown to the parties. Both parties were ignorant of the loss at perfection, so fortuity subsists. The subject is therefore insurable, subject to insurable interest and the other requisites.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 1. Definition of Insurance Contract

section: 2. Principal Object and Purpose Test (HMO Product; Variable Contracts)
stem: An HMO sells cards guaranteeing doctor visits for a fixed fee, and it absorbs all costs even during epidemics. Is it doing an insurance business?
answer: Yes, the HMO is doing an insurance business in substance and is answerable to regulation. Under the Section 2(b) substance test, absorption of fortuitous cost for consideration is risk assumption. Here, epidemic overuse is the contingent event, and the fixed fee is the consideration. The HMO is therefore doing an insurance business in substance.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 2. Principal Object and Purpose Test (HMO Product; Variable Contracts)

section: 3. Doing an Insurance Business; Mutual Insurance Companies
stem: A civic club pools member contributions and pays fire losses of members, with no profit and no commission. Is it doing an insurance business?
answer: Yes, the club is doing an insurance business. Section 2(b)(1) governs, together with the no-profit sentence: absence of profit does not negate the business. Here, pooling contributions and paying members' fire losses is indemnity on a contingency, regardless of profit motive. The club therefore needs a certificate of authority, and unlicensed operation is punishable.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 3. Doing an Insurance Business; Mutual Insurance Companies

section: 4. Applicable Laws (New Civil Code; Corporation Code)
stem: The policy is silent on when a mailed renewal binds. Which law answers?
answer: The Civil Code answers, through the cognition rule in Article 1319. The Civil Code applies suppletorily where the Insurance Code is silent. A mailed acceptance therefore binds only upon the offeror's knowledge. The renewal is effective when the insurer knew of the acceptance.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 4. Applicable Laws (New Civil Code; Corporation Code)

section: 5. Importance of Insurance; Dealing with Risks
stem: Why can the insurer pay P45M on one fire (cf. Cebu Shipyard) and stay solvent?
answer: The insurer stays solvent through pooling. Insurance rests on the distribution of losses across the pool. Here, the single large loss is funded by the premiums of the many exposures. Solvency therefore rests on spread, pricing, and reserves.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 5. Importance of Insurance; Dealing with Risks

section: 6. Characteristics (Indemnity; Not a Wagering Contract)
stem: A P5M building is insured for P3M and suffers a P1.5M partial fire loss under a 60 percent coinsurance clause. What is the recovery?
answer: Recovery is scaled down. The insured does not get the full P1.5M. Under Galian's ratable-proportion rule and the Section 17 measure, the insurer pays only the insured proportion of the loss. Here, the insured carried part of the risk by underinsuring the P5M building for P3M. The insurer therefore pays only the coinsured proportion of the loss.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 6. Characteristics (Indemnity; Not a Wagering Contract)

section: 7. Perfection (Requisites, Cognition, Offer/Acceptance, Unaccepted Application, Stipulation, Tort Liability, Delivery)
stem: "Jason is the proud owner of a newly-built house worth PS million. As a protection against any possible loss or damage to his house, Jason applied for a fire insurance policy thereon with Shure Insurance Corporation (Shure) on October 11, 2016 and paid the premium in cash. It took the company a week to approve Jason's application. On October 18, 2016, Shure mailed the approved policy to Jason which the latter received five (5) days later. However, Jason's house had been razed by fire which transpired a day before his receipt of the approved policy. Jason filed a written claim with Shure under the insurance policy. Shure prays for the denial of the claim on the ground that the theory of cognition applies to contracts of insurance. Decide Jason's claim with reasons. (5%)"
answer:
Jason's claim must fail on these facts because no contract had yet been perfected when the fire occurred.
Perfection needs absolute acceptance known to the offeror: mailed acceptance binds only from knowledge under Civil Code Article 1319, paragraph 2, and the policy here was still in transit at loss.
Approval was mailed October 18 and was received five days later. The fire came the day before receipt, so at loss no acceptance had reached Jason and no contract yet existed despite premium payment.
Shure is correct to deny. The premium is returnable. Delay alone neither perfects the contract nor, without inexcusable neglect proved, makes a tort case on these facts.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 7. Perfection (Requisites, Cognition, Offer/Acceptance, Unaccepted Application, Stipulation, Tort Liability, Delivery)

section: 8. Kinds of Insurance; Kinds of Property Insurance Policy
stem: Two fire policies cover the same building, with the owner holding one and the lessee holding the other, and both are disclosed. Is there a forfeiture?
answer: No, there is no forfeiture, and both policies stand. Forfeiture needs triple identity of subject, interest, and risk, and La O holds that different interests defeat the clause. Here, the owner's interest and the lessee's interest differ. Both policies therefore stand, and the loss is shared within each policy's measure.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 8. Kinds of Insurance; Kinds of Property Insurance Policy

section: 10. The Policy (Form, Basic Provisions, Identification, Adhesion, Interpretation, Indivisibility, Proof, Riders, Cover Notes, Renewal, Reformation)
stem: A policy insures "Building A", and the insurer denies a claim on Building B by invoking an unsigned, unattached, and unreferred-to endorsement. Does that endorsement form part of the contract?
answer: The endorsement is no part of the contract. Riders must be attached to the policy, referred to in it, and supported by premium, and ambiguities are construed against the insurer. Here, the unsigned, unattached, and unmentioned endorsement binds no one. The Building A claim therefore stands on the policy as written.

section: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)
stem: "(c) Insurable interest in property (2%)".
answer:
Insurable interest in property is any interest in property, whether real or personal, or any relation thereto, or liability in respect thereof, of such nature that a contemplated peril might directly damnify the insured.
The governing provisions are Section 13 for the definition, Section 18 requiring that the policy be enforceable only for one holding such interest, Section 19 fixing the time at both effect and loss, and Section 17 fixing the measure at damnification.
The question asks for the bare definition, which the Section 13 sentence supplies.
A complete answer therefore recites the Section 13 definition together with the Section 19 timing and the Section 17 measure.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)

section: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)
stem: "Emilio owns a car which he purchased from Gregorio. Emilio agreed to pay Gregorio the balance of the purchase price in the amount of P500,000 within one year. To secure the payment of the balance, Emilio and Gregorio executed a security agreement that complies with the requirements of the Personal Property Security Act (PPSA). The security interest was also perfected in accordance with the PPSA. Who has insurable interest over the car? Explain your answer."
answer:
Both Emilio and Gregorio hold insurable interest over the car.
Section 13's property interest covers any damnifiable relation to the thing. Section 14 reaches existing interests and expectancies coupled with an existing interest. A perfected PPSA security interest is such a relation.
Emilio as buyer-owner holds the existing ownership interest. Gregorio as perfected secured creditor holds an interest to the extent of the P500,000 collectible from the car.
Either or both may therefore insure, each within its own measure (Sec. 17), and two policies on different interests are no double-insurance breach (La O and 2025-5).
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)

section: 12. Premium (Accrual, Provision, Forms, Non-Payment, Check, Binding Despite Unpaid, Lapse Prevention, Return, Rebate)
stem: "Flavio obtained from Safe Assurance Corporation (SAC), through its agent Laureen, a fire insurance policy over his residential house for a period of one year from August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025. Flavio delivered on August 26, 2024 a check representing premium payment to Laureen who then issued an acknowledgment receipt. On August 27, 2024, a fire completely razed Flavio's house. Oblivious of the incident, Laureen deposited the check on August 28, 2024 to SAC's bank account and was credited on the same day. Thereafter, Flavio filed against SAC an insurance claim. However, SAC denied the claim and argued that there was no payment of premium yet to make the insurance policy effective at the time of the loss. SAC explained that it received the premium payment only on August 28, 2024 or after the fire occurred on August 27, 2024. Is there a valid and binding insurance contract between SAC and Flavio? Explain."
answer:
Yes, a valid and binding insurance contract exists between SAC and Flavio, and SAC must pay the claim.
A premium delivered to the authorized agent with an acknowledgment receipt is payment to the insurer. Cover attaches upon perfection plus exposure within the policy period. Later bank crediting does not move the payment date back.
Flavio paid by check to Laureen on August 26, inside the August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025 term, and the receipt placed payment before the August 27 fire, which fell within cover. The August 28 deposit is merely internal timing.
The denial therefore fails: the contract is valid and the loss is covered.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 12. Premium (Accrual, Provision, Forms, Non-Payment, Check, Binding Despite Unpaid, Lapse Prevention, Return, Rebate)

section: 1. Cancellation; Rescission
stem: N, a non-life insurer, sent a cancellation notice for a fire policy five days before termination, citing a ground not listed in Sec. 64. The insured demanded the facts and received none. May the insurer treat the policy as cancelled?
answer:
No, the attempted cancellation is ineffective and the policy remains in force until validly cancelled or otherwise terminated.
Under Sec. 64 cancellation after effectivity is allowed only on seven exclusive statutory grounds, and under Sec. 65 it requires prior written notice stating the ground with a right in the insured to demand the supporting facts.
Here the notice gave a short five-day lead, invoked an unlisted ground, and the insurer ignored the demand for facts, so both the substantive ground and the procedural notice requirements fail.
The cancellation has no effect. The insurer remains bound and any denial on the basis of that cancellation will fail.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 1. Cancellation; Rescission

section: 2. Ascertaining and Controlling Risks
stem: P applied for marine cargo cover and disclosed the voyage route but not the well-known port congestion surcharge practice. The insurer asked no question on surcharges, issued the policy, then sought rescission for concealment. Will rescission prosper?
answer:
No, rescission will not prosper because the undisclosed practice was equally open to inquiry and within general usage of trade.
Under Sec. 28 there is no duty to communicate what the other has the means of ascertaining, and under Sec. 32 each party is bound to know general causes open to inquiry and general usages of trade, with waiver by neglect to inquire under Sec. 33.
Here the surcharge practice was a general usage equally accessible to the insurer, the voyage disclosure implied added cost exposure, and the insurer neglected to inquire, so the fact was either bound-to-know or waived.
There is no concealment of a material fact the insurer could not ascertain, so the policy stands and rescission fails.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 2. Ascertaining and Controlling Risks

section: 3. Concealment
stem: Diego, a cancer survivor, filed an application for a life insurance policy with Garantiya Insurance Company (GIC). He delivered his application and insurance premium to Gabriela, the officer of GIC in charge of approving life insurance policies. Gabriela then approved the application of Diego on June 1, 2020. On January 30, 2023, Diego died in a vehicular accident. When the heirs of Diego claimed the insurance proceeds, GIC denied the claim on the ground that Diego had concealed the fact of his illness. Moreover, Gabriela knew about the illness of Diego but also concealed it from GIC. Is the denial of the insurance claim by GIC proper? Discuss.
answer:
No, the denial is improper and the heirs may recover because the insurer is deemed to have known the illness through its approving officer and cannot claim concealment.
Under Secs. 26 to 28 and 31 concealment is neglect to communicate a known material fact the other has no means of ascertaining, judged by probable influence on underwriting, while knowledge of an agent in charge of approval is knowledge of the insurer and Sec. 33 waives inquiry neglected where the fact was knowable.
Here Gabriela, the officer in charge of approving life policies, knew of the cancer history when she approved the application on June 1, 2020, so GIC had the means of ascertaining and is charged with that knowledge, and death by later vehicular accident confirms materiality is not judged by the event.
There is no concealment against GIC, waiver and estoppel bar avoidance, and the claim denial fails so proceeds must be paid.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 3. Concealment

section: 4. Representation
stem: A applied for fire insurance stating the warehouse was "concrete-walled" when it was half timber, but added "per my caretaker, who I have not verified." The policy as issued expressly describes the building as "concrete throughout." May the insurer rescind, and may A invoke the caretaker explanation?
answer:
Yes, the insurer may rescind if the falsity is material, and A cannot defeat rescission by pointing to the caretaker source or by using the representation to contradict the express policy term.
Under Secs. 44–46, a representation is false when facts fail to correspond with its assertions, falsity in a material point entitles the injured party to rescind, and materiality follows concealment rules. Sec. 40 bars a representation from qualifying an express provision, and the Sec. 43 second-hand-information excuse fails when the source is the insured's agent whose duty is to inform or when no source explanation cures a material misstatement of own fact.
The timber construction contradicts the concrete assertion so the representation is false. A concrete-vs-timber wall plainly affects underwriting and is material. Because the policy expressly states concrete throughout, the representation cannot qualify or soften that term. The caretaker remark does not shift responsibility where A adopted the statement as his own to obtain cover.
The insurer is entitled to rescind from the time the representation became false, subject to proof of materiality at trial.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 4. Representation

section: 5. Warranties
stem: A fire policy warrants "two 2.5-inch hydrants with 100 psi at all times." At issuance the insurer inspects, sees one weak hydrant, issues anyway, and collects premiums for two years. After a fire, may it avoid solely for breach of that warranty with no fraud shown?
answer:
No, the insurer cannot avoid on that warranty alone where it knew the true condition and accepted premiums, and without fraud Sec. 76 gives only exoneration-while-breached rather than automatic avoidance.
Secs. 74–76 distinguish material breach entitling rescission from immaterial breach that does not avoid absent policy declaration, and a non-fraudulent breach merely exonerates from occurrence or prevents attachment if broken in inception. Qua Chee Gan adds waiver and estoppel where the insurer knew the deficiency and took premiums, with uberrimae fidei and contra-proferentem against the insurer.
The hydrant warranty is material on its face, but the insurer's prior inspection and continued premium collection estop it from invoking a condition it knowingly wrote over a known non-compliance. With no fraud, Sec. 76 does not let it treat the whole policy as void ab initio for a supervening shortfall.
The breach defense fails on estoppel and waiver. The insurer remains liable subject to any valid Sec. 73 excuse analysis, which does not help it here.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 5. Warranties

section: 6. Conditions; Other Insurance Clause
stem: A insures factory machines with X containing an other-insurance clause, then secretly insures the same machines with Y against the same fire risk for an overlapping period. Separately, the X policy says suit must be filed within 6 months of loss. After fire, X invokes both defenses. Decide each defense.
answer:
X wins on the other-insurance breach but loses on the 6-month suit limit, which is void, leaving the insured the lawful period to sue.
Breach of an other-insurance condition forfeits where the same subject matter, same interest, and same risk concur with non-disclosure under Multi-Ware, while La O requires all three and recognizes waiver. Sec. 63 voids any policy condition limiting suit to less than one year from accrual.
The Y policy hits all three identities on the same machines, same ownership interest, and same fire peril, so non-disclosure breaches the X clause with no waiver shown. The 6-month limit falls below the Sec. 63 floor and is void, leaving the insured the lawful period to sue.
Forfeiture on the co-insurance ground stands, but the time-bar defense fails as void under Sec. 63.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 6. Conditions; Other Insurance Clause

section: 7. Exclusion/Exception; Burden of Proof
stem: In January 2016, Mr. H was issued a life insurance policy by XYZ Insurance Co., wherein his wife, Mrs. W, was designated as the sole beneficiary. Unbeknownst to XYZ Insurance Co., however, Mr. H had been previously diagnosed with colon cancer, the fact of which Mr. H had concealed during the entire time his insurance policy was being processed. In January 2019, Mr. H unfortunately committed suicide. Due to her husband's death, Mrs. W, as beneficiary, filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Co. to recover the proceeds of the late Mr. H's life insurance policy. However, XYZ Insurance Co. resisted the claim, contending that: 1. the policy is void ab initio because Mr. H fraudulently concealed or misrepresented his medical condition, i.e., his colon cancer; and 2. as an insurer in a life insurance policy, it cannot be held liable in case of suicide. Rule on each of XYZ Insurance Co.'s contentions. (5%)
answer:
Contention 2 fails. The January 2019 suicide, about three years after the January 2016 issue, falls outside any suicide exclusion.
Under Sec. 183 the insurer in a life contract is liable for suicide committed after the policy has been in force two years from issue or last reinstatement, and exclusions are strictly construed against the insurer, which bears the burden of proving the exception after the beneficiary's prima facie case.
The policy ran from January 2016 to January 2019, about three years, so the two-year suicide threshold is passed and XYZ proved no insanity issue or shorter policy period. Its blanket citation of suicide, without clause or proof, cannot carry an exclusion defense that is construed against it.
Contention 2 is denied and XYZ is liable on this ground, subject to the §8 incontestability analysis that independently bars contention 1.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 7. Exclusion/Exception; Burden of Proof

section: 8. Incontestable Clause
stem: In January 2016, Mr. H was issued a life insurance policy by XYZ Insurance Co., wherein his wife, Mrs. W, was designated as the sole beneficiary. Unbeknownst to XYZ Insurance Co., however, Mr. H had been previously diagnosed with colon cancer, the fact of which Mr. H had concealed during the entire time his insurance policy was being processed. In January 2019, Mr. H unfortunately committed suicide. Due to her husband's death, Mrs. W, as beneficiary, filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Co. to recover the proceeds of the late Mr. H's life insurance policy. However, XYZ Insurance Co. resisted the claim, contending that: 1. the policy is void ab initio because Mr. H fraudulently concealed or misrepresented his medical condition, i.e., his colon cancer; and 2. as an insurer in a life insurance policy, it cannot be held liable in case of suicide. Rule on each of XYZ Insurance Co.'s contentions. (5%)
answer:
Contention 1 is barred. XYZ cannot prove void ab initio or rescindibility for fraudulent concealment after 3 years in force.
Sec. 48 bars proof of void ab initio or rescindibility by fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation after a life policy payable on death has been in force during the insured's lifetime for 2 years from issue or last reinstatement, with rescission required before action on the contract.
The policy was issued in January 2016 and was in force until death in January 2019, about 3 years during Mr. H's lifetime. Colon-cancer concealment is exactly the fraud defense that Sec. 48 cuts off, and void-ab-initio styling does not evade it per *Manila Bankers*.
XYZ must pay as to contention 1. Its remedy was timely investigation and pre-action rescission within 2 years.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 8. Incontestable Clause

section: 9. War Limitation Rider / War Clause
stem: Cargo insured under marine policy with F.C. and S. clause deleted and Institute War Clauses attached is seized by civil authority. Insurer denies, citing the war exclusion in the printed form. Rule on the denial.
answer: The insurer is liable because civil arrest is covered under the policy as rewritten. Sec. 88 excepts only perils especially excepted as written, and the deleted F.C. and S. language plus the added Institute War Clauses restore war-risk coverage strictly construed in the insured's favor. Deletion erased the printed war exclusion and the rider affirmatively covered civil arrest, so the insurer cannot revive deleted text and has not proved a surviving exception. The insurer must therefore pay the claim because the war defense fails on the policy as rewritten.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 9. War Limitation Rider / War Clause

section: 10. Defenses of Insured against Revocation
stem: Insurer learns of concealment in Year 1, keeps collecting premiums for a year, then after loss and after beneficiary sues, declares rescission. The insured pleads waiver, estoppel, and timeliness. Rule on the defenses.
answer: All three defenses succeed, so rescission is barred and the insurer must pay. Knowing premium collection waives forfeiture, conduct inducing reliance estops contradiction, and Sec. 48 requires rescission previous to action on the contract. One year of post-knowledge collection shows intentional relinquishment and induced reliance, and the post-suit rescission violates the previous-to-action rule, with incontestability as an added bar if the life-policy and 2-year requisites are met. Rescission is therefore ineffective because the insurer is barred by waiver, estoppel, and timeliness.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 10. Defenses of Insured against Revocation

section: 1. Loss
stem: Absolute Timber Co. (ATC) has been engaged in the logging business in Isabela. To secure one of its shipments of logs to be transported by Andok Shipping Co., ATC purchased a marine policy with an "all risks" provision. Because of a strong typhoon then hitting Northern Luzon, the vessel sank and the shipment of logs was totally lost. ATC filed its claim, but the insurer denied the claim on several grounds, namely: (1) the vessel had not been seaworthy; (2) the vessel's crew had lacked sufficient training; (3) the improper loading of the logs on only one side of the vessel had led to the tilting of the ship to that side during the stormy voyage; and (4) the extremely bad weather had been a fortuitous event. ATC now seeks your legal advice to know if its claim was sustainable. What is your advice. Explain your answer. (3 percent)
answer:
The claim is sustainable. An all-risks marine policy covers all fortuitous losses proximately caused by perils of the sea unless expressly excepted, and the typhoon sinking is the proximate cause of total loss.
Sec. 86 holds the insurer liable where the insured peril was the proximate cause though an uncontemplated peril was remote. Sec. 89 provides that negligence of the insured or its agents does not exonerate. Under Pan Malayan a sunken cargo valueless to the owner is actual total loss payable in full.
Defenses 1 to 3 sound in unseaworthiness, manning, and loading negligence, which Sec. 89 keeps inside coverage. Defense 4 concedes that the insured peril itself caused the sinking. No excepted peril was invoked under the Sec. 88 but-for test.
Denial is improper. The insurer is liable for the total loss.
authorities: Part I-C Loss Settlement Subrogation.md :: 1. Loss

section: 2. Notice of Loss
stem: A fire policy requires written notice within 15 days. The insured notifies on day 40 without justification, then cures a defective proof after the insurer specifies the defect late. Run Secs. 90, 92, and 93 and conclude which omission exonerates the insurer and which omission it waived.
answer: The insurer is exonerated for the late fire notice under Sec. 90, because forty days without justification exceeds without unnecessary delay, unless the delay was insurer-caused or went unobjected under one of the two Sec. 93 waivers. The proof defect specified late is waived under Sec. 92, since a defect the insurer failed to specify without delay cannot later defeat the claim. The notice delay therefore bars recovery unless waived, while the late-specified defects do not bar it.
authorities: Part I-C Loss Settlement Subrogation.md :: 2. Notice of Loss

section: 3. Collateral Source Rule
stem: The insured's employer pays sick-leave benefits for the same confinement the health insurer covers. The insurer deducts the sick-leave amount. Decide, then explain where the insurer's real recourse lies.
answer: The deduction is improper because the sick-leave pay comes from a source independent of the insurer, so the collateral source rule requires the health policy to pay in full with total recovery capped at the loss. Employer benefits and policy proceeds answer different promises, and Secs. 95-96 deduction and contribution apply only to same-person same-interest co-insurance. The insurer must therefore pay the policy in full, and any recourse runs through subrogation against the party liable for the loss, never by deduction from the insured.
authorities: Part I-C Loss Settlement Subrogation.md :: 3. Collateral Source Rule

section: 4. Claims Settlement
stem: A non-life insurer receives complete proof of loss on March 1, neither agrees on the amount nor arbitrates within 60 days, and pays on day 120, blaming heavy volume. The insured sues for the proceeds plus damages. Decide interest and damages.
answer: The insurer owes double-ceiling interest from May 31, the day after the 90-day Sec. 249 deadline fixed at May 30 where ascertainment defaulted, until full satisfaction, because heavy volume is not just cause and missing the deadline is prima facie unreasonable delay under Sec. 250. Payment on day 120 is therefore 30 days of delay with no fraud defense pleaded. The insured recovers the proceeds plus double-ceiling interest, attorney's fees, and proven expenses.
authorities: Part I-C Loss Settlement Subrogation.md :: 4. Claims Settlement

section: 5. Prescriptive Period
stem: A fire policy requires suit within six months of the fire. The insured sues in month eight after a denied claim. The insurer pleads the six-month clause. Decide.
answer: The six-month suit clause is void under Sec. 63 because it falls below the one-year-from-accrual floor, reckoned from accrual which here postdates the fire, so the insurer's plea fails. The suit filed in month eight is proper, and the insurer must defend on the merits.
authorities: Part I-C Loss Settlement Subrogation.md :: 5. Prescriptive Period

section: 6. Subrogation
stem: X obtained an insurance policy for her Porsche Carrera GT from XYZ Insurance Company. The same car was insured by her creditor-mortgagee, Y, with ABC Insurance Company. When the car was damaged because of an accident, X filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Company. The latter denied the claim since it discovered that the car was also insured with ABC Insurance Company. According to XYZ Insurance Company, double insurance is prohibited by law. Decide with reason(s).
answer:
Denial is improper. Double insurance exists only where the same person is insured by several insurers separately in respect to the same subject and interest, and X and Y are different persons with distinct interests (owner vs creditor-mortgagee).
Sec. 95 defines double insurance, and under Malayan v Phil First the same goods and the same peril for different persons with distinct insurable interests is not double insurance, so the other-insurance and contribution clauses do not apply.
X's policy answers her ownership interest while Y's answers the mortgage-credit interest. XYZ must pay X's claim and, having paid, is subrogated under Art. 2207 against the party at fault for the accident. Any over-indemnity is adjusted by Sec. 96 deduction and ratable contribution.
XYZ is liable on the policy. Double insurance is regulated and apportioned, not prohibited.
authorities: Part I-C Loss Settlement Subrogation.md :: 6. Subrogation

section: 1. Reinsurance
stem: X obtained an insurance policy for her Porsche Carrera GT from XYZ Insurance Company. The same car was insured by her creditor-mortgagee, Y, with ABC Insurance Company. When the car was damaged because of an accident, X filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Company. The latter denied the claim since it discovered that the car was also insured with ABC Insurance Company. According to XYZ Insurance Company, double insurance is prohibited by law. Decide with reason(s).
answer:
Denial of the claim is improper because X and Y are different persons with distinct interests — owner and creditor-mortgagee — so the two policies are not double insurance, which exists only where the same person is insured by several insurers separately in respect to the same subject and interest.
The controlling rule is Sec. 95, which defines double insurance by the same-person, same-subject, same-interest identities, as applied in Malayan v Phil First: the same goods exposed to the same peril but insured for different persons with distinct interests is not double insurance, and double cover is regulated by deduction and contribution under Sec. 96, not prohibited.
Applied here, XYZ answers X's ownership interest while ABC answers Y's mortgage-credit interest, so each insurer pays on its own contract without deduction from the other.
XYZ is therefore liable on X's claim, and neither an other-insurance clause nor Sec. 96 contribution defeats recovery.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 1. Reinsurance

section: 2. Fire Insurance
stem: Flavio obtained from Safe Assurance Corporation (SAC), through its agent Laureen, a fire insurance policy over his residential house for a period of one year from August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025. Flavio delivered on August 26, 2024 a check representing premium payment to Laureen who then issued an acknowledgment receipt. On August 27, 2024, a fire completely razed Flavio's house. Oblivious of the incident, Laureen deposited the check on August 28, 2024 to SAC's bank account and was credited on the same day. Thereafter, Flavio filed against SAC an insurance claim. However, SAC denied the claim and argued that there was no payment of premium yet to make the insurance policy effective at the time of the loss. SAC explained that it received the premium payment only on August 28, 2024 or after the fire occurred on August 27, 2024. Is there a valid and binding insurance contract between SAC and Flavio? Explain.
answer:
Yes, a valid and binding insurance contract exists between SAC and Flavio because delivery of the premium check to the insurer's authorized agent, evidenced by the August 26 acknowledgment receipt, perfected payment as between insured and insurer, and the August 27 loss fell within the August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025 cover.
The controlling rules are that cash-and-carry is satisfied by payment to the authorized agent whose receipt binds the insurer, and that Sec. 173 measures the razed house at the replacement expense at the commencement of the fire.
Applied here, Flavio paid through Laureen before the fire razed the house, so SAC's August 28 bank-credit date is a mere internal matter that does not move the payment date, and the denial on the no-premium ground fails.
SAC is therefore liable for the fire loss.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 2. Fire Insurance

section: 2. Fire Insurance
stem: Jason pays in cash Oct. 11. The insurer mails the approved policy Oct. 18. Fire razes the house before receipt. Decide under perfection and assumption-of-risk rules and state the measure under Sec. 173.
answer: The insurer is liable because the contract was perfected on approval and the risk had already attached before the fire, since Jason's October 11 cash payment and the insurer's approval perfected the contract so the October 18 mailing did not defer attachment of the risk, and the insurer must therefore pay the replacement expense of the house in the condition it was in at the time of the injury under Section 173.

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: In January 2016, Mr. H was issued a life insurance policy by XYZ Insurance Co., wherein his wife, Mrs. W, was designated as the sole beneficiary. Unbeknownst to XYZ Insurance Co., however, Mr. H had been previously diagnosed with colon cancer, the fact of which Mr. H had concealed during the entire time his insurance policy was being processed. In January 2019, Mr. H unfortunately committed suicide. Due to her husband's death, Mrs. W, as beneficiary, filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Co. to recover the proceeds of the late Mr. H's life insurance policy. However, XYZ Insurance Co. resisted the claim, contending that: 1. the policy is void ab initio because Mr. H fraudulently concealed or misrepresented his medical condition, i.e., his colon cancer; and 2. as an insurer in a life insurance policy, it cannot be held liable in case of suicide. Rule on each of XYZ Insurance Co.'s contentions. (5%)
answer:
Both of XYZ's contentions fail because by January 2019 the policy had been in force for three years, so the Sec. 48 two-year incontestability bar kills the concealment defense and the Sec. 183 two-year suicide clock makes the suicide compensable.
The controlling rules are Sec. 48, under which the insurer is barred after two years from proving void ab initio or rescission for fraud or concealment even on a void-ab-initio recast (Manila Bankers), and Sec. 183, which makes the insurer liable for suicide committed after the policy has been in force two years from issue or last reinstatement.
Applied here, three years in force exceeds both clocks, so the concealed colon cancer can no longer be proved to avoid the policy and the sane suicide after the period is a covered risk.
XYZ must therefore pay Mrs. W the proceeds of the policy.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: On June 21, 2008, Yate took out a life insurance policy on her life in the amount of PhP 10 million and named her husband Vandy and daughter as joint irrevocable beneficiaries. Before the policy was issued and the premiums were paid, Yate underwent a medical checkup with a physician accredited by the insurer, and the only result found was that she was suffering from high blood pressure. Yate was previously diagnosed by a private physician of having breast cancer which she did not disclose to the insurer in her application, nor to the insurer's accredited physician because by then, she was told that she was already cancer-free after undergoing surgery which removed both her breasts. She was later diagnosed with psychotic tendency that graduated into extreme despondency. She was found dead hanging in her closet 36 months after the issuance of the policy. The police authorities declared it to be a case of suicide. The policy did not include suicide as an excepted risk. (a) Can the insurer raise the issue of failure to disclose that she had cancer as a cause for denying the claim of the beneficiaries? (2.5%) (b) Are the beneficiaries entitled to receive the proceeds of the life insurance notwithstanding the fact that the cause of death was suicide? (2.5%)
answer:
(a) No, the insurer cannot raise the non-disclosure of the breast cancer because thirty-six months in force exceeds the two-year incontestability period, so that defense is barred. (b) Yes, the beneficiaries are entitled to the proceeds because suicide thirty-six months after issue is compensable under Sec. 183, the policy did not except suicide, and insanity-graded despondency reinforces compensability.
The controlling rules are Sec. 48 as construed in Manila Bankers and the Sec. 183 suicide text quoted above.
Applied here, the insurer's own accredited examination found only hypertension, so the cancer history, even if material, is time-barred, and the 36-month suicide falls outside any exclusion window.
Vandy and the daughter therefore recover the P10M as joint irrevocable beneficiaries.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: Shortly after Yin and Yang were wed, they each took out separate life insurance policies on their lives, and mutually designated one another as sole beneficiary. Both life insurance policies provided for a double indemnity clause, the cost for which was added to the premium rate. During the last 10 years of their marriage, the spouses had faithfully paid for the annual premiums over the life policies from both their salaries. Unfortunately, Yin fell in love with his officemate, Vessel, and they carried on an affair. After two years, their relationship bore them a daughter named Vinsel. Without the knowledge of Yang, Yin changed the designation of the beneficiary to an "irrevocable designation" of Vinsel and Vessel jointly. When Yang learned of the affair, she was so despondent that, having chanced upon Yin and Vessel on a date, she rammed them down with the car she was driving, resulting in Vin's death and Vessel's complete loss of mobilization. Yang was sued for parricide, and while the case was pending, she filed a claim on the proceeds of the life insurance of Yin as irrevocable beneficiary, or at least his legal heir, and opposed the claims on behalf of Vessel and her daughter Vinsel. Yang claimed that her designation as beneficiary in Vin's life insurance policy was irrevocable, in the nature of one "coupled with interest," since it was made in accordance with their mutual agreement to designate one another as sole beneficiary in their respective life policies. She also claimed that the beneficiary designation of Vessel and the illegitimate minor child Vinsel was void being the product of an illicit relationship, and therefore without "insurable interest." (a) Is Yang correct in saying that her designation as beneficiary was irrevocable? (2.5%) (b) Do Vessel and Vinsel have "insurable interest" on the life of Yin? (2.5%)
answer:
(a) No, Yang is not correct because a beneficiary designation is revocable unless expressly made irrevocable in the policy, a private mutual agreement does not create irrevocability "coupled with interest," and Yin's later express irrevocable designation of Vinsel and Vessel displaced her. Her killing of Yin additionally disqualifies her as beneficiary. (b) Vessel and Vinsel need no insurable interest on Yin's life because Sec. 184 lets a life policy pass to any person and Sec. 10 gives Yin insurable interest in his own life to support naming whom he pleases, so their illicit origin does not void the designation itself.
The controlling rules are Secs. 184-185, which allow transfer to any person without need of notice, together with the revocability default and the killer-beneficiary disqualification.
Applied here, ten years of faithful premium payment created no vested irrevocability, so the written irrevocable change controls and Vessel and Vinsel take as designated transferees.
Yang's irrevocability claim therefore fails, and Vessel and Vinsel may recover as irrevocable beneficiaries, subject to the parricide consequence against Yang.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: X insured his life for P20 million. X, plays golf and regularly exercises everyday, hence is considered in good health. He did not know, however, that his frequent headache is really caused by his being hypertensive. In his application form for a life insurance for himself, he did not put a check to the question if he is suffering from hypertension, believing that because of his active lifestyle, being hypertensive is a remote possibility. While playing golf one day, X collapsed at the fairway a [question continues in the official release on hypertension concealment and materiality]. [a] Will the beneficiary of X be entitled to the proceeds of the life insurance under the circumstances, despite the non-disclosure that he is hypertensive at the time of application? (2.5%) [b] If X died in an accident instead of a heart attack, would the fact of X's failure to disclose that he is hypertensive be considered as material information? (2.5%)
answer:
[a] The beneficiary's right to the proceeds depends on good faith and materiality at application, because unknowing non-disclosure without fraudulent intent does not avoid the policy where the applicant genuinely believed himself healthy, but hypertension that caused the very death is material and avoids the policy if it is proved to have been known or fraudulently concealed. [b] No, the undisclosed hypertension is not a ground to deny the accidental-death claim because immateriality to accidental death means it would not have affected the risk assumed.
The controlling rules are that concealment avoids only when fraudulent and material to the risk, that incontestability under Sec. 48 (Manila Bankers) bars late proof after two years, and that Biagtan distinguishes accidental from non-accidental death measures.
Applied here, X's good-faith omission plus the insurer's own medical-examination opportunity weigh against avoidance, and death by accident severs any causal link to hypertension.
The insurer must therefore pay where the omission was innocent or time-barred, and may deny only on proved fraudulent material concealment within the contestable period.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: The insured names his business partner, who has no insurable interest, as irrevocable beneficiary, then outlives two years. Decide on the partner's right and the insurer's late fraud defense.
answer: The business partner recovers the proceeds because Section 184 lets a life policy pass to any person even without insurable interest, so the irrevocable designation stands, and the insurer's fraud suit comes too late because Section 48 bars rescission after two years in force.

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: An insured with two successive marriages names both wives as beneficiaries. State who takes and why, running Secs. 184-185 and the revocability default.
answer: The widow named in the last valid written designation takes the proceeds because beneficiary designations are revocable by default so the later designation displaces the earlier one, each taker needs no insurable interest under Sections 184 and 185, and the succession of marriages itself neither supplies nor defeats the designation.

section: 4. Annuity
stem: X transfers P1,000,000 to Y in exchange for a yearly pension during the life of Z, who dies of a pre-existing illness ten days after the contract. X demands the capital back. Decide under Arts. 2021-2024.
answer: The constitution is void and X recovers the capital because Z died within twenty days from a pre-existing illness under Article 2023, so no valid measuring life ever attached and the Article 2024 arrears-only remedy for a valid annuity never came into play.

section: 5. Casualty Insurance
stem: A personal accident policy excludes ten listed causes. The insured dies in a stabbing by strangers, with no provocation. The insurer denies the claim. It cites an unlisted peace-and-order exclusion it says is implied. Decide whether the insurer must pay.
answer: The insurer must pay the face amount because the death is accidental as to the insured under the Section 176 trigger, murder by strangers falls outside the ten listed causes so the exclusive enumeration closes against adding an implied peace-and-order exclusion, and ambiguities construe against the insurer.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 5. Casualty Insurance

section: 6. Compulsory Motor Vehicle Liability Insurance (CMVLI)
stem: A pedestrian is hit by a private car. Sworn police report and hospital receipts for P40,000 are filed with the offending car's insurer. The insurer refuses any payment until fault is proved and demands a full quitclaim for P15,000. The victim sues eight months after denial. Decide liability, amount floor, quitclaim, and prescription.
answer:
The insurer must pay no-fault indemnity of at least P15,000.00 on the sworn papers without proof of fault, and it may not condition payment on a full quitclaim, while the balance above the floor is litigated on fault and the suit filed eight months after denial is within the Sec. 397 one-year period.
The controlling rules are Sec. 391(a)-(c) on the no-fault track, the Sec. 398 first paragraph barring quitclaim compulsion, and Sec. 397 on the six-month notice and one-year-from-denial suit.
Applied here, the sworn police report plus medical and disbursement proof satisfies Sec. 391(b), Sec. 391(c) points the claim at the directly offending vehicle, Sec. 398 bars the forced quitclaim, and eight months from denial is inside the one-year limit.
The insurer must therefore pay no-fault now, litigate the excess on fault, and the action is timely.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 6. Compulsory Motor Vehicle Liability Insurance (CMVLI)

section: 7. Marine Insurance
stem: A time-policy hull insurer denies a mid-period voyage loss because the ship, seaworthy at inception of the period, developed unseaworthiness during an earlier voyage that the master unreasonably delayed repairing. The cargo owner separately claims although the hull was sound for hull purposes. Decide both claims.
answer:
The hull claim fails for losses arising from the unrepaired defect because Sec. 117(a) demands seaworthiness at the commencement of every voyage and Sec. 120 exonerates the insurer on unreasonable delay in repairing unseaworthiness, while the cargo claim depends on Sec. 121, under which fitness for hull purposes does not decide fitness for cargo.
The controlling rules are Secs. 115-121 as quoted and tabled above.
Applied here, the master's unreasonable delay in repair triggers the Sec. 120 exoneration on the resulting hull loss, and cargo seaworthiness is separately measured at the inception of the risk against equipment, lading, and manning.
The denial is therefore proper on the resulting hull loss, and cargo recovery turns on cargo-specific unseaworthiness.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 7. Marine Insurance

section: 8. Suretyship
stem: EFG, Inc. is indebted to Bank Y in the amount of P50,000,000.00. The loan was secured by a suretyship agreement issued by Z Insurance Co. Due to EFG, Inc's default, Bank Y filed a case against Z Insurance Co. as surety. There is also a pending criminal case for violation of the Bouncing Checks Law against the President of EFG, Inc., Mr. P, who signed the check as signatory for the company. Unable to meet its obligations as they fell due, EFG, Inc. filed a petition for rehabilitation. Finding the petition sufficient in form and substance, the court issued a Commencement Order, which was thereafter published. (a) Should the case filed against Z Insurance Co. be suspended in light of the Commencement Order? Explain. (2.5%) (b) Should the criminal case filed against Mr. P be suspended in light of the Commencement Order? Explain. (2.5%)
answer:
(a) No, the case against Z Insurance Co. should not be suspended because the surety's liability is joint and several with the obligor under Sec. 178 and solidary under Art. 2047, second paragraph, so Bank Y may proceed directly against the surety while the rehabilitation stay covers only EFG, with the solidary surety answering independently up to the bond amount. (b) No, the criminal case against Mr. P should not be suspended because rehabilitation suspends only enforcement of civil claims against the debtor, while his criminal liability for the Bouncing Checks Law violation is personal to him as signatory and is not a claim against EFG's estate.
The controlling rules are Sec. 178 on joint-and-several liability within the bond cap and strict bond terms, Art. 2047 on solidary suretyship, and Arts. 2059(2) and 2084 on the absence of exhaustion where the obligation is solidary or the bond is judicial.
Applied here, Bank Y sues on the surety's independent solidary promise and not on EFG's stayed obligation, and Mr. P is prosecuted for his own act of issuing the worthless check and not for EFG's debt.
Neither case is therefore suspended: Bank Y collects from Z up to the bond amount, and the State prosecutes Mr. P.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 8. Suretyship

section: 8. Suretyship
stem: Yellow Fin Tuna Corporation (Yellow Fin), a domestic corporation, applied for a credit facility in the amount of PhP 50 million with Yengzi Financial Corporation (YFC). The application was approved and the Credit Agreement was signed and took effect. Ysko and Yuan, Yellow Fin Chairman and President, respectively, executed a Continuing Suretyship Agreement in favor of YFC wherein they guaranteed the due and full payment and performance of Yellow Fin's guarantee obligations under the credit facility. YFC soon discovered material inconsistencies in the financial statements given by Yellow Fin, drawing YFC to conclude that Yellow Fin committed misrepresentation. Under the Credit Agreement, any misrepresentation by Yellow Fin or its sureties will constitute an event of default. YFC thus called an event of default and filed a complaint for sum of money against Yellow Fin, Ysko, and Yuan. Immediately thereafter, Yellow Fin filed a petition for rehabilitation. The court suspended the proceedings in YFC's complaint until the rehabilitation court disposed of the petition for rehabilitation. YFC posits that the suspension of the proceedings should only be with respect to Yellow Fin but not with respect to Ysko and Yuan. Is YFC correct? (2.5%)
answer:
Yes, YFC is correct because a continuing suretyship guarantees full payment and performance of present and future obligations under the facility under Art. 2053, and sureties bind themselves solidarily under Sec. 178 and Art. 2047, so YFC may enforce directly against Ysko and Yuan despite the stay on Yellow Fin, with the solidary sureties answering on their own promise and remaining suable while retaining reimbursement against the debtor later under Arts. 2066-2067.
The controlling rules are Art. 2053 on future debts secured, Sec. 178 and Art. 2047 on joint-and-several and solidary liability, and Art. 2059(2) on the absence of excussion where the obligation is solidary.
Applied here, Ysko and Yuan signed a continuing solidary guarantee of the whole facility, so YFC's declaration of default on misrepresentation triggered their independent liability, unaffected by Yellow Fin's rehabilitation stay.
Suspension is therefore proper as to Yellow Fin only, and the complaint proceeds against Ysko and Yuan.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 8. Suretyship

section: 1. Insurance Commissioner
stem: Villacorta leaves her insured car with a repair shop for check-up and repairs. A shop employee drives it to Montalban without her consent, crashes it into a parked truck, and the car is extensively damaged. The insurer invokes the authorized-driver clause and denies theft, and the Insurance Commission dismisses her complaint on those grounds. Decide whether recovery lies and state the appeal route.
answer:
The claim is recoverable under both the authorized-driver and theft covers, so the Commission's dismissal of the own-damage and theft claim must be set aside.
The controlling rules are Sec. 439, which lets the Commissioner adjudicate the insured's own-damage and theft claim up to P5,000,000.00 with appeal by notice to the Court of Appeals within thirty (30) days. The adhesion-construction rule resolves policy ambiguities strictly against the insurer. Art. 308 of the Revised Penal Code treats unlawful taking without consent as theft because use itself is gain.
Applied here, entrusting the key to an established repair shop presumptively authorizes legitimate driving by a licensed driver, so the diversion to an illicit purpose does not breach the clause. The taking without consent is theft regardless of permanence, and here it proved lasting since the car was smashed beyond serviceable return.
Villacorta therefore recovers P35,000.00 with legal interest from filing, subject to the insurer's subrogation against the shop, and the remedy from the adverse ruling is a Sec. 439 notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals filed with the Commissioner within thirty (30) days from receipt.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 1. Insurance Commissioner

section: 2. Regulations Imposed on Insurance Business
stem: A new domestic non-life insurer with P800,000,000.00 paid-up capital and facially complete papers applies for a certificate of authority, and the Commissioner considers refusing it. Decide whether the certificate may issue and state the refusal ground.
answer:
No certificate may issue on these papers, and the Commissioner may additionally refuse any application where refusal best promotes the interest of the people of the country.
The controlling rules are Sec. 194, which requires at least P1,000,000,000.00 in paid-up capital for a new stock life or non-life company, kept unimpaired for continuance. Sec. 193 bars issuance until the Commissioner is satisfied on the four requisites of Philippine-law qualification, local economic justification, sound direction and administration with integrity, and financial organization and capital reasonably assuring the safety of policyholders and the public.
Applied here, P800,000,000.00 falls short of the P1,000,000,000.00 floor regardless of papers. Even at full capital, economic justification, management integrity, and policyholder safety must each still be satisfied.
The application must therefore be denied on the capital floor alone, and refusal is likewise lawful on an adverse best-interest judgment under Sec. 193.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 2. Regulations Imposed on Insurance Business

section: 3. Regulation of Persons Involved in the Business
stem: A non-life insurer controlled by H Corp. proposes to sell to H Corp. an asset worth 6 percent of its admitted assets as of Dec. 31 last year without asking anyone. H Corp. separately buys 45 percent of the insurer's voting stock without notice. Decide whether either transaction may proceed under Secs. 290, 299, and 302.
answer:
Both transactions are barred as proposed because each crosses a control-line threshold that needs prior clearance.
The controlling rules are Sec. 290(b), which presumes control where a person holds forty percent (40%) or more of voting securities. Sec. 299 requires prior written approval for a controlled insurer's transactions with its holding-company system involving five percent (5%) or more of admitted assets. Sec. 302(a) requires twenty (20) days written notice plus prior written approval for a non-insurer's acquisition of control of a domestic insurer.
Applied here, the six-percent asset sale exceeds the five-percent line and falls outside the thirty-day notice band for smaller transactions, while the forty-five-percent stock purchase exceeds the forty-percent presumption and is an acquisition of control by a non-insurer.
Neither transaction may therefore proceed without the required approvals: prior written approval for the sale, and twenty-day notice plus prior written approval for the acquisition.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 3. Regulation of Persons Involved in the Business

section: 4. Insurers in Financial Distress
stem: The Commissioner places troubled insurer X under conservatorship. X argues the Commissioner should have gone straight to liquidation because its books look insolvent. State the correct sequencing answer with reasons.
answer:
Conservatorship was the correct first step because rehabilitation must be tested before any winding up.
The controlling sequence runs from Sec. 254 suspension through Sec. 255 conservatorship on continuing inability or unwillingness to stay solvent or liquid, to Sec. 256 receivership with cease-and-desist on disclosed insolvency or hazardous continuance, with liquidation only upon the ninety (90)-day determination that the insurer is insolvent or cannot safely resume and the public interest requires it.
Applied here, books that merely look insolvent call for examination with suspension or conservation rather than immediate winding up, while the receiver gathers and administers assets during the ninety-day reorganization inquiry.
Conservatorship therefore stands, receivership and liquidation follow only as the escalation matures, and a liquidated insurer is never rehabilitated or reauthorized.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 4. Insurers in Financial Distress

section: 5. Rate Regulation
stem: Insurer Y charges a favored client 20 percent below its last-filed rate and pays the client's manager an unstated cash inducement. Y then seeks to charge a hazardous risk 30 percent above file without asking. Decide which acts violate Secs. 365, 366, and 370 and which can still be cured.
answer:
All three acts were unlawful as done, and only the surcharge can still be cured.
The controlling rules are Sec. 365, which bars charging, demanding, or receiving any rate deviating from the last filing. Sec. 370 absolutely prohibits any off-policy rebate, special favor, or unstated inducement to the insured or its employee. Sec. 366 permits a higher-than-filed rate on a specific risk only upon a written application stating reasons, filed with and approved by the Commissioner.
Applied here, the twenty-percent discount is deviation regardless of motive, the unstated cash to the client's manager is a rebate, and the thirty-percent surcharge was charged without the required reasoned written approval.
The discount and the inducement therefore stand as violations, while only the surcharge is curable through a Sec. 366 application filed and approved before use.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 5. Rate Regulation

section: 1. Defined; Governing Law and State Policy; Insurance Commission
stem: A hospital gives subscribers, their spouses, and dependents free or discounted board, procedures, and drugs as subscriber incentives. Decide whether these perks are pre-need plans or HMO contracts.
answer:
The perks are neither pre-need plans nor HMO contracts. They are mere shareholder incentives.
The controlling rules are Sec. 4(b) of RA 9829, which requires a contract for future service, money, or benefit at actual need or agreed maturity in exchange for cash or installment amounts. EO 192 s. 2015 defines an HMO contract as pre-agreed health care services for a fixed prepaid fee over a period through a provider network.
Applied here, the perks ride on stock subscription payments rather than plan consideration and promise no benefit at actual need or agreed maturity. They likewise involve no fixed prepaid fee and no provider network.
The perks therefore fall outside both Sec. 4(b) and the HMO definition and stand as mere shareholder incentives.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 1. Defined; Governing Law and State Policy; Insurance Commission

section: 2. Parties; Other Regulated Persons; Suspension/Revocation
stem: A company offers pension plans online with bank-deposit payment instructions but holds no license. Decide whether the offer is actionable.
answer:
The online offer is actionable, and a cease-and-desist order against it is proper.
The controlling rules are Sec. 10, which bars operation as a pre-need company without a Commission license. Sec. 18 requires prior Commission approval of advertising. Sec. 53(c) fines unauthorized sales on a 30%/40%/license-loss ladder. Sec. 54(a)-(b) punishes unregistered selling with one (1) year of imprisonment and triple-price fines.
Applied here, the Primamanila-pattern facts — a website offer of pension plans with bank-deposit payments and no license — breach both the licensing gate and the advertising gate.
The Commission may therefore issue a cease-and-desist order, and fines plus criminal exposure attach.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 2. Parties; Other Regulated Persons; Suspension/Revocation

section: 3. Kinds of Plans; Pre-need Contract and Interpretation
stem: After a planholder's mother dies, the family at once engages an outside funeral home that embalms the body and supplies a casket, notifies the provider only that evening, and later substitutes a different casket. Decide whether the provider owes memorial services.
answer:
The provider owes no memorial services, and the dismissal of the claim stands.
The controlling rules are that the plan is the law between the parties so its clear stipulations control literally, and that Sec. 3 liberality for the planholder cannot rewrite those stipulations.
Applied here, the sole-and-exclusive arrangement right and the imperative acknowledged-notice requirement were preempted by the evening notice after embalming and casketing, and the pre-selected-casket term was breached by the upgrade whose cost falls on the family alone.
There is therefore no liability for refusing the services, and the CA dismissal stands.

section: 4. Registration/Disclosure; Consideration
stem: A planholder misses six months of installments after receiving only one notice, and the company cancels the plan. Decide whether the cancellation is valid.
answer:
The cancellation is invalid, and the company must accept reinstatement or reimburse the late payments.
The controlling rule is Sec. 23, which requires a 60-day grace period, a 2-year reinstatement window from grace lapse with no cancellation inside it, and two written 30-day notices — one after grace expiry and one after reinstatement-period expiry.
Applied here, six months of nonpayment still falls inside the reinstatement window, and a single notice fails the two-notice rule.
Cancellation is therefore barred until the window closes with both notices given. The company must accept reinstatement or reimburse.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 4. Registration/Disclosure; Consideration

section: 5. Termination (by Planholder; by Company)
stem: A pre-need company offers to buy out plans at 120 percent of termination value without Commission approval, and some planholders object. Decide whether the offer may proceed.
answer:
The offer cannot proceed as to the objecting planholders without Commission approval.
The controlling rule is Sec. 24, which requires a fair, equitable, Commission-compliant termination-value schedule predetermined by the actuary and disclosed in the contract, and which allows a company above-value offer without prior approval only where the consideration is below the plan's pre-need reserves, the planholder accepts, and non-availing planholders are not prejudiced.
Applied here, the objectors defeat both the acceptance and non-prejudice conditions, and below-reserves proof is still required.
The offer therefore cannot proceed as to objectors and must be routed through Commission approval.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 5. Termination (by Planholder; by Company)

section: 6. Claims Settlement; Unfair Claims Settlement
stem: A matured education plan pays 60 days late without any fraud. State what the beneficiary collects.
answer:
The beneficiary collects twice-legal-interest for the delay period plus Sec. 28 damages on suit.
The controlling rules are Sec. 26, which prices scheduled-plan delay at twice legal interest from day 16 where the planholder complied with documents. Sec. 28 imposes actual damages, attorney's fees, and legal interest from claim date on unreasonable withholding, with a missed Sec. 26 clock as prima facie proof of unreasonable delay.
Applied here, the 60-day delay yields 45 days of delay interest, and the missed clock supplies the prima facie case for litigation damages if unreasonableness is found.
The beneficiary therefore recovers twice-legal-interest for the delay period plus Sec. 28 damages on a successful suit.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 6. Claims Settlement; Unfair Claims Settlement

section: 7. Trust Fund; Regulation of Companies; Companies in Distress
stem: General creditors of an insolvent pre-need company seek to attach the trust fund. Decide whether attachment lies.
answer: The attachment fails, and the creditors are confined to non-fund assets. The controlling rules are Sec. 30, which bars diversion of the fund and creditor claims against it notwithstanding any contrary law. Sec. 52 excludes the fund from court insolvency jurisdiction and denies creditors personality in Commission fund proceedings. Laigo vests beneficial ownership of the fund in the planholders. Applied here, the attachment targets fund assets, the precise object of the statutory shield. Attachment therefore fails, and creditors may proceed against non-fund assets only.

section: 1. Definition; Parties; Elements; Perfection
stem: Wisconsin Transportation Co., Inc. (WTC) owned and operated an inter-island de luxe bus service plying the Manila-Batangas-Mindoro route. Three friends, namely: Aurelio, Jerome and Florencio rode on the same WTC bus from Manila bound for Mindoro. Aurelio purchased a ticket for himself. Jerome, being a boyhood friend of the bus driver, was allowed a free ride by agreeing to sit during the trip on a stool placed in the aisle. Florencio, already penniless after spending all of his money on beer the night before, just stole a ride in the bus by hiding in the on-board toilet of the bus. During the trip, the bus collided with another bus coming from the opposite direction. The three friends all suffered serious physical injuries. What are WTC's liabilities, if any, in favor of Aurelio, Jerome and Florencio? Explain your answer. (4%)
answer:
WTC answers to Aurelio and Jerome as its passengers and owes nothing to Florencio as a stowaway outside the contract.
Aurelio holds a ticket and Jerome rides by the driver permission inside the vehicle, so both entered carriage by consent while Florencio boarded by stealth without the carrier acceptance that perfection requires.
WTC must therefore carry Aurelio and Jerome with the utmost diligence of very cautious persons, and their injuries raise the presumption of fault that yields only to proof of extraordinary diligence.
Florencio cannot invoke the contract since no meeting of minds ever bound him to the carrier, so he recovers only if he proves the ordinary negligence that the law demands of every person.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 1. Definition; Parties; Elements; Perfection

section: 2. Common Carriers: Tests, Characteristics, Ancillary Business, Exclusions
stem: LMN, Inc. operates a beach resort in a secluded island off the coast of Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. It operates three (3) motorized boats to ferry its guests from the city proper to the island resort and vice-versa. During one rainy morning, the guests were informed that the ferry services for that day were cancelled due to a storm forecast. In order to appease the apparent dismay of most of the guests who will miss their flight back to Manila, the boat captain of one of LMN, Inc.'s motorized boats decided to push through with its trip back to the city. Shortly after the boat sailed, the storm hit and the winds and waves became stronger, causing engine trouble to the boat. Unfortunately, the boat capsized and sank, resulting in the death of one of the passengers, Mr. X. This prompted Mr. X's heirs to file a complaint for damages against LMN, Inc., which they alleged to be a common carrier. In its defense, LMN, Inc. maintained that it is not a common carrier because its boats are not available to the general public but only ferry resort guests and employees. (a) May LMN, Inc. be considered a common carrier? Explain. (3%) (b) Assuming LMN, Inc. is a common carrier, may it be absolved from liability on the ground of fortuitous event? Explain. (2%)
answer:
LMN, Inc. is a common carrier and it is not absolved by the storm, since it sailed into a known danger and the law imputes the package fare as compensation.
Its boats carry guests by water for the imputed fare inside the resort package, and Art. 1732 reaches ancillary and narrow-client carriage so long as the service is offered to whoever books the resort.
The storm defense fails because the forecast preceded the sailing and the captain chose to brave it, which keeps the human fault concurrent with the waves and defeats the fortuity claim.
Death therefore raises the presumption of fault, and only proof of extraordinary diligence could rebut it, which a voluntary voyage into a forecasted storm cannot supply.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 2. Common Carriers: Tests, Characteristics, Ancillary Business, Exclusions

section: 3. Effect of Charter Party
stem: Onassis Shipping, Inc. (Onassis) operated passenger vessels and cargo trucks, and offered its services to the general public. In line with its vision and mission to protect the environment, Go-Green Asia (Go-Green), an NGO affiliated with Greenpeace, entered into a contract with Onassis whereby Go-Green would operate with its own crew the MN Dolphin, an ocean-going passenger vessel of Onassis. While on its way to Palawan carrying Go-Green's invited guests who were international and local observers desirous of checking certain environmental concerns in the area, the MN Dolphin encountered high waves and strong winds caused by a typhoon in the West Philippine Sea. The rough seas led to serious physical injuries to some of the guests. Discuss the liabilities of Onassis and Go-Green to the passengers of the M/V Dolphin. Explain briefly your answer. (3%)
answer:
Go-Green answers as the carrier for the voyage while Onassis keeps owner exposure under its public franchise, since the contract transferred crew and command to Go-Green.
The transfer of operation with its own crew marks a demise in substance, which makes Go-Green the private operator for the invited guests and lifts the voyage out of Onassis common-carrier performance.
Go-Green therefore bears the diligence of the carrier in command, and the typhoon excuses only if it stood alone without concurrent fault in braving known rough seas.
Onassis remains reachable on registered ownership and franchise responsibility even as Go-Green carries the primary voyage liability to the injured guests.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 3. Effect of Charter Party

section: 4. Common vs Private Carrier; vs Towage, Arrastre, Stevedoring, Travel Agency
stem: To celebrate her 70th birthday, A hired F Travel & Tours to arrange and facilitate her booking, ticketing, and accommodation for a two-week foreign tour, which included visits to Italy and Greece, for the total amount of PHP 145,000.00. On Wednesday, August 14, 2024, B, an employee of F Travel & Tours, went to A's house to deliver the travel documents and plane ticket. She told A to be at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) on Saturday, August 17, 2024 two hours before her flight schedule. Without checking her travel documents, A went to NAIA on Saturday, August 17, 2024. When she got there, she was informed that the flight she was supposed to take had already left the previous day. A demanded that F Travel & Tours refund her payment. She claimed that F Travel & Tours did not observe the standard of care required of a common carrier when its employee, B, informed her of the wrong flight schedule. Is F Travel & Tours liable as a common carrier? Reason(s).
answer:
F Travel & Tours is not liable as a common carrier, though it may answer for its own fault as an agent.
It never undertook carriage over any route and never held itself out as transporting the public, since it only arranged bookings, tickets, and hotels for the celebrant.
The extraordinary diligence and presumed fault of Arts. 1733 and 1735 to 1756 therefore never attached, because those burdens follow the carrier undertaking and not the arranging work.
Its employee gave the wrong flight date, so liability if any rests on agency fault proved by the traveler and not on the carrier presumption she invoked.

section: 5. Tramp vs Line Service; Governing Laws; Nature of Business
stem: A liner keeps a fixed Manila-Cebu schedule for whoever books, while a tramp takes whatever bulk cargo offers under voyage charters to chosen charterers. A shipper asks which vessel answers as a common carrier if its cargo is lost. How do you advise?
answer:
The liner answers as the common carrier while the tramp answers as the private carrier on these facts.
The liner holds scheduled carriage out to the public for pay, which meets Art. 1732 without need of further proof of regularity or purpose.
The tramp serves chosen charterers by special contract without a public offer, which places it under charter and Code of Commerce rules with fault to be proved.
The shipper therefore sues the liner under the presumption of fault and sues the tramp on proved willful negligence, since schedules only evidence and never replace the holding-out test.

section: 6. Registered Owner Rule and Kabit System; Boundary System
stem: A bus is sold but the sale is never registered, and the buyer ties the unit to the seller franchise under a kabit arrangement with the driver on boundary. A passenger is hurt when the bus collides with a truck. From whom may the passenger recover?
answer:
The passenger may recover from the registered franchise holder, who cannot hide behind the unregistered sale or the illegal tie-up.
Registration tells the public who operates the vehicle, so the seller on record answers although beneficial ownership already passed to the buyer.
The kabit pact is void between the operators, yet that voidness never travels to the victim since pari delicto bars only the wrongdoers against each other.
The boundary setup keeps the operator as employer, so the driver fault in the collision is the operator fault that the presumption of carrier negligence already provisionally establishes.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 6. Registered Owner Rule and Kabit System; Boundary System

section: 7. Formalities: Bill of Lading
stem: A carrier issues a clean bill of lading for bagged fertilizer in apparent good order, and the consignee receives short and hardened bags at discharge. The carrier points to a printed clause exempting it from all liability for any loss. Is the bill conclusive and is the clause valid?
answer:
The clean bill proves prima facie fault for the shortage and the blanket exemption is void.
The bill admits receipt in apparent good order, so short and deteriorated delivery raises the presumption that the carrier failed in extraordinary diligence.
The printed total-exemption clause asks less than the diligence the law commands, and stipulations that erase carrier responsibility fall as contrary to public policy.
The carrier therefore answers for the shortage unless it proves an excepted cause with extraordinary care, since the bill fixes the prima facie case and the void clause contributes nothing to the defense.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 7. Formalities: Bill of Lading

section: 1. Duty to Accept Goods; Grounds for Refusal; Animals
stem: A shipper tenders drums of nitric acid in brittle crates for a Friday sailing, plus fighting cocks in flimsy coops. The carrier refuses both. A second shipper tenders bagged fertilizer in sound sacks for the same sailing and is also refused for lack of space though room can be made. Which refusals stand?
answer:
The acid and the cocks refusals stand while the fertilizer refusal fails, since lawful ground excuses while convenience never does.
The acid is dangerous cargo in unfit packing and the coops are unfit for live carriage, so both tenders fall outside what the carrier must take until disclosure, safeguards, and fit containers cure them.
The fertilizer is ordinary cargo in sound packing within the advertised run, so tight space alone is no lawful ground where the carrier holds itself out for such goods.
The carrier therefore answers for the fertilizer refusal and keeps its refusal of the acid and the birds until proper tender is made.
