section: 2. Timely Delivery; Place of Delivery; To Whom Delivered
stem: A consignee lost the original bills and presents certified copies, then signs delivery receipts for each lot through his clerks. Months later the shipper sues the carrier for non-delivery, blaming the missing originals. Is the carrier discharged?
answer:
The carrier is discharged, since signed receipts by the entitled recipient stand in for the missing originals.
The agents substantially complied by demanding the bills and documenting each turnover, which proves the extraordinary diligence that rebuts the fault presumption.
The shipper left its own supervisor unpursued until resignation, so it cannot pass to the carrier what may have been its own employee faithlessness.
The non-delivery claim therefore fails while the carrier keeps no liability for the lots duly receipted.

section: 2. Timely Delivery; Place of Delivery; To Whom Delivered
stem: Hari and Reyna booked a honeymoon package at Anya Resort (AR) in Palawan which included transportation from Batangas to Palawan, and vice versa, via M/B Prinsesa owned and operated by AR. Despite PAGASA storm warning bulletins, M/B Prinsesa proceeded to ferry Hari and Reyna from the port of Batangas to Palawan. While in open seas, the boat was hit by big waves and eventually capsized, drowning Hari and Reyna. When sued by the heirs of the couple, AR denied liability on the ground that it is not a common carrier, as M/B Prinsesa is not available to the general public or other tourists, and exclusively ferries resort guests and crew members. AR further argued that they did not charge Hari and Reyna separate fees to board M/B Prinsesa. Are the arguments of AR correct? Discuss your answer.
answer:
The arguments of AR are incorrect, since the resort boat is a common carrier and sailing into the storm breached its utmost diligence.
The boat carries guests by water for the imputed fare inside the package, and Art. 1732 reaches ancillary and narrow-client carriage so long as the service is offered to whoever books the resort.
The storm defense fails because the bulletins preceded the sailing and the captain chose to brave them, which keeps the human fault concurrent with the waves and defeats the fortuity claim.
Death therefore raises the presumption of fault, and only proof of extraordinary diligence could rebut it, which a voluntary voyage into a forecasted storm cannot supply.

section: 4. Extraordinary Diligence: Rationale, Meaning, Presumption, Duration, and Stipulations
stem: Ysidro, a paying passenger, was on board Bus No. 904 owned and operated by Yatco Transportation Company (Yatco). He boarded the bus at Munoz, Nueva Ecija with Manila as his final destination. He was seated on the first row, window seat on the left side of the bus. As the bus was negotiating the national highway in front of the public market of Gerona, Tarlac, the bus came to a full stop because of the traffic. The driver of the bus took this opportunity to check on the tires of the bus and to relieve himself. As he was alighting from the bus to do these, an unidentified man standing along the highway hurled a huge rock at the left side of the bus and hit Ysidro between his eyes. He lost consciousness and immediately the driver, with the conductor, drove the bus to bring him to the nearest hospital. He expired before the bus could reach the hospital. Ysidro's wife and children brought a civil action to collect damages from Yatco, alleging that as a common carrier, it was required to exercise extraordinary diligence in ensuring the safety of its passengers. They contended that, in case of injuries and/or death on the part of any of its passengers, the common carrier is presumed to be at fault. In its defense, Yatco alleged that it is not an absolute insurer of its passengers and that Ysidro's death was not due to any defect in the means of transport or method of transporting passengers, or the negligent acts of its employees. Since the accident was due to the fault of a stranger over whom the common carrier had no control, or of which it did not have any prior knowledge to be able to prevent it, the cause of Ysidro's death should be considered a fortuitous event and not the liability of the common carrier. (a) Is a common carrier presumed to be at fault whenever there is death or injury to its passengers, regardless of the cause of death or injury? (2.5%) (b) What kind of diligence is required of common carriers like Yatco for the protection of its passengers? (2.5%) (c) Will your answer be the same as your answer in (b) above, if the assailant was another paying passenger who boarded the bus and deliberately stabbed Ysidro to death? (2.5%)
answer:
A carrier is presumed at fault on a passenger death or injury, yet the presumption yields to proof of utmost diligence, and a stranger attack still tests what diligence could have prevented.
The law presumes fault or negligence on death or injury under Art. 1756, so the carrier opens every case carrying the burden of proving the extraordinary diligence of Arts. 1733 and 1755.
That diligence is the utmost care of very cautious persons with due regard for all the circumstances, and the carrier is no absolute insurer since an unforeseeable stranger act it could not have prevented with good-family vigilance breaks liability under Art. 1759.
A fellow-passenger stabbing is judged the same way, since the carrier answers only where its employees could have prevented or stopped the assault through the diligence the law demands.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 4. Extraordinary Diligence: Rationale, Meaning, Presumption, Duration, and Stipulations

section: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea
stem: Nautica Shipping Lines (Nautica) bought a second hand passenger ship from Japan. It modified the design of the bulkhead of the deck of the ship to accommodate more passengers. The ship sunk with its passengers in Tablas Strait due to heavy rains brought by the monsoon. The heirs of the passengers sued Nautica for its liability as a common carrier based on the reconfiguration of the bulkhead which may have compromised the stability of the ship. Nautica raised the defense that the monsoon is a fortuitous event and, at most, its liability is prescribed by the Limited Liability Rule. Decide with reasons. (5%)
answer:
Nautica answers as a common carrier and keeps neither the fortuity defense nor the limited-liability cap on these facts.
The bulkhead reconfiguration that may have compromised stability puts seaworthiness in issue, and ordinary monsoon rains are voyage vicissitudes rather than an irresistible calamity standing alone.
The storm defense needs an excepted cause with extraordinary diligence, yet sailing a possibly unstable rebuilt ship with passengers aboard proves the opposite of the diligence the law demands.
The abandonment privilege then fails with it, since the owner whose own fault concurred with the casualty cannot limit liability to vessel and freight.
## 6. Extraordinary Diligence by Land and Train; Railroad Crossings

section: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea
stem: A railroad track of the Philippine National Railway (PNR) is located near a busy intersection of Puyat Avenue and Osmeña Highway. One afternoon, the intersection was heavily congested, as usual. Juan, the driver of a public utility jeepney (PUJ), drove onto the railroad tracks but could go no farther because of the heavy traffic at the intersection. After the jeepney stopped right on the railroad track, it was hit and overturned by a PNR train, resulting in the death of Kim, a passenger of the PUJ, and injuries to Juan and his other passengers. Juan, the injured passengers and Kim's family sued the PNR for damages for its negligence. It was established that the steel pole barrier before the track was broken, and that the PNR had the last clear chance of avoiding the accident. On the other hand, the PNR raised the defense that the track is for the exclusive use of the train and that motorists are aware that it is negligence per se to stop their vehicles on the tracks. Decide the case and explain. (5%)
answer:
The PNR answers though Juan was also at fault, since the broken barrier and the last clear chance keep the train operator liable while Juan fault never travels to his passengers.
The carrier and operator owe utmost diligence over the line with working warnings, and a barrier left broken at a known congested crossing breaches that diligence before any jeepney stalls.
Juan breached his own motorist duty by entering rails he could not clear, so his personal claim suffers his contributory fault under the avoidable-consequences and last-clear-chance sorting.
Kim and the riding passengers recover in full, since the driver negligence is not imputed to them and the PNR with the final opportunity to stop must answer for the injuries its train inflicted.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea

section: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea
stem: A bus company hires an unlicensed driver without road test, skips brake inspection for a month, and the bus with worn pads rams a truck. The company blames the truck driver. Who answers the injured bus passengers?
answer:
The bus company answers the passengers, since its own want of diligence concurs regardless of the truck fault.
Hiring without license or test breaches selection diligence and skipping brake checks breaches inspection diligence, so the presumption of fault stands unrebutted.
The truck fault may divide the ultimate loss between the operators through contribution, yet division never delays or defeats the passenger recovery.
The passengers therefore collect from their carrier upon the presumption, and the company pursues the truck operator separately for its share.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea

section: 7. Passenger Baggage
stem: A tagged suitcase checked into the hold vanishes before arrival, while a laptop kept in the overhead bin is snatched when the passenger leaves it to use the lavatory. What must each claimant prove?
answer:
The suitcase claimant proves turnover with loss at arrival while the laptop claimant must prove carrier fault, since custody fixes the burden.
The tagged suitcase rode in carrier custody, so vanishing baggage raises the presumption of fault and the carrier must prove extraordinary diligence or an Art. 1734 excuse.
The laptop stayed in passenger custody throughout, so no presumption runs and the passenger must show the snatching came through employee fault or want of due precautions.
The first claim therefore succeeds on custody and loss alone unless rebutted, while the second needs specific fault proved against the carrier.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 7. Passenger Baggage

section: 8. Obligations of the Passenger and Shipper
stem: A shipper declares general merchandise but hides drums of calcium carbide that explode on contact with seawater, damaging fellow cargo. He then refuses freight, claiming the carrier failed to deliver. Who pays for the damage and the freight?
answer:
The shipper pays for the damage and still owes the freight, since concealment caused the casualty while carriage was duly performed.
The undisclosed dangerous character is shipper fault under Art. 1734(3) that breaks the carrier chain, so the explosion loss falls on the concealing shipper with recourse from him by the fellow cargo owners.
The carrier earned its freight by receiving, stowing, and sailing the goods with the diligence the known facts demanded, so refusal to pay has no basis in the failed-delivery claim.
The carrier therefore keeps its lien on surviving goods for the unpaid charges while the shipper answers for the explosion damage.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 8. Obligations of the Passenger and Shipper

section: 8. Obligations of the Passenger and Shipper
stem: A passenger boards without a visa for the destination state and is refused onward carriage at the transit stop. He demands a full refund and damages for delay. Does he collect?
answer:
He collects no damages though fare rules decide the refund, since travel papers are his own duty.
Passports, visas, and health papers belong to the passenger under his Art. 1761 self-care and the contract terms, and want of them lawfully excuses carriage without breach.
Delay from the refusal is therefore his own making rather than carrier fault, so no delay damages run.
The carrier keeps the flown legs earned and refunds only what its tariff promises for the unflown portion.

section: 1. Kinds of Defenses; Proximate Causation
stem: LMN, Inc. operates a beach resort in a secluded island off the coast of Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. It operates three (3) motorized boats to ferry its guests from the city proper to the island resort and vice-versa. During one rainy morning, the guests were informed that the ferry services for that day were cancelled due to a storm forecast. In order to appease the apparent dismay of most of the guests who will miss their flight back to Manila, the boat captain of one of LMN, Inc.'s motorized boats decided to push through with its trip back to the city. Shortly after the boat sailed, the storm hit and the winds and waves became stronger, causing engine trouble to the boat. Unfortunately, the boat capsized and sank, resulting in the death of one of the passengers, Mr. X. This prompted Mr. X's heirs to file a complaint for damages against LMN, Inc., which they alleged to be a common carrier. In its defense, LMN, Inc. maintained that it is not a common carrier because its boats are not available to the general public but only ferry resort guests and employees. (a) May LMN, Inc. be considered a common carrier? Explain. (3%) (b) Assuming LMN, Inc. is a common carrier, may it be absolved from liability on the ground of fortuitous event? Explain. (2%)
answer:
LMN, Inc. is a common carrier, yet it keeps no fortuity defense since its own decision to sail concurred with the storm.
The boats ferry guests by water for the imputed fare inside the resort package, and narrow clientele never defeats common character where the service is held out to whoever books the resort.
The storm was forecasted and the service stood cancelled, so sailing to appease guests with engine trouble mid-voyage keeps human fault beside the waves and breaks the proximate-and-only-cause demand of Art. 1739.
Death therefore raises the presumption of fault, and only proof of utmost diligence could rebut it, which a voluntary voyage into a forecasted storm cannot supply.

section: 2. Defenses in Carriage of Goods in Their Exclusivity and in Carriage of Passengers
stem: A vessel loses bagged coffee to warehouse rats during a tariff stop while a passenger on the same voyage is hurt by a falling hatch cover. The carrier pleads unlisted vermin for the coffee and talks of open rebuttal for the passenger. Which plea follows the correct structure?
answer:
Both pleas name the right structure, yet each still needs its own proof to succeed.
The coffee claim runs through the closed goods list, so rats fit nothing in Art. 1734 and the Art. 1735 presumption stands unless the carrier proves extraordinary diligence over the stored bags.
The passenger claim runs through open rebuttal, so the carrier may show hatch inspection with maintenance records and utmost care, which can defeat the Art. 1756 presumption.
The carrier therefore likely pays for the coffee while keeping a fighting chance on the passenger fall.

section: 3. Fortuitous Event with Carrier Participation, Rationale, Fire, Storm, Hijacking, Mechanical Defects, Tire Blowouts, and Other Invalid Defenses
stem: A warehouse holding consigned sugar burns from an unknown origin at night while a bus with bald tires blows one on the highway and topples. The warehouseman pleads fire and the bus line pleads blowout. Which plea has a path and what must each prove?
answer:
The fire plea has a narrow path while the blowout plea has almost none, since diligence decides both.
Fire sits outside the five Art. 1734 causes, so the warehouseman carrier stays presumed at fault and must prove extraordinary diligence with watchmen, wiring, extinguishers, and segregation fully shown.
The bald tires prove want of roadworthiness by themselves, so the blowout is carrier-side unfitness rather than calamity and the presumption stands unrebutted.
The sugar claim therefore turns on the diligence proof while the bus claim fails on the treads alone.

section: 3. Fortuitous Event with Carrier Participation, Rationale, Fire, Storm, Hijacking, Mechanical Defects, Tire Blowouts, and Other Invalid Defenses
stem: Scrap iron rides a carrier lighter when an acting mayor with armed men orders the crew to dump it into the sea as part of a shakedown of the shipper. The carrier obeys and pleads competent authority. Does the excuse stand?
answer:
The excuse fails, since a lawless shakedown order is no competent authority.
The carrier must prove official power with a lawful order with issuance under legal process, and a mayor pressing a money demand over goods the town never owned supplies none of the three.
Obedience was carrier fault rather than legal duty, since the scraps could have been unloaded ashore and delivered after the dispute instead of dumped.
The line therefore answers under the Art. 1735 presumption with no diligence proved, following Ganzon v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. L-48757, 1988).

section: 3. Fortuitous Event with Carrier Participation, Rationale, Fire, Storm, Hijacking, Mechanical Defects, Tire Blowouts, and Other Invalid Defenses
stem: Bulk urea sails in sealed holds with intact seals and arrives short with part contaminated by sand after eleven days of rainy unloading by consignee labor under free-in-and-out terms. The consignee sues for shortage and pollution. Who bears the loss?
answer:
The consignee bears the loss, since goods character with shipper-side handling caused it despite a diligent voyage.
Urea solubility with bulk spillage risk is inherent character under Art. 1734(4), and the sealed hatches with clean holds prove the extraordinary care the voyage demanded.
Unloading belonged to the cargo interests under the agreed terms, so rainy open-air handling with sandy hauling falls outside carrier custody fault.
The presumption therefore stands rebutted and the claim fails, following Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, 1993).

section: 5. Defenses in Carriage of Passengers; Acts of Employees, of Other Passengers and Third Persons, and of Shipper or Passenger
stem: A conductor pockets a sleeping passenger watch while a stranger at a traffic stop hurls a rock through the window and blinds another rider. The line pleads stranger fortuity for both losses. How does liability divide?
answer:
The line answers for the watch and tests the rock by preventability, since employees and strangers run on different articles.
The pocketed watch is a wilful employee act under Art. 1759 though against orders, and no hiring diligence or ticket term escapes it under Art. 1760.
The rock is stranger harm under Art. 1763, so the line answers only where good-family crew vigilance with closed windows, guards, or route care could have prevented or stopped it.
Theft therefore pays as of course while the blinding turns on the prevention proof.

section: 6. Notice of Claim and Prescription in Overland and Coastwise Shipping, in International Carriage by Sea, and in Subrogation
stem: A consignee receives crates by truck with intact exteriors, opens them after three days to find water damage, and complains on the fifth day. A second consignee receives container cargo by foreign vessel, joins the survey at receipt, then sues ten months after discharge. Which claims live?
answer:
The truck claim dies on notice while the vessel claim lives on joint survey with suit inside the year.
Intact exteriors mean concealed damage, so Art. 366 demanded complaint within twenty-four hours from receipt and the fifth-day notice with freight paid bars the condition claim.
Joint survey at vessel receipt excuses the COGSA writing, and suit ten months after discharge sits inside the one-year period that late notice could never shorten.
The first consignee therefore loses procedurally while the second reaches the merits.

section: 6. Notice of Claim and Prescription in Overland and Coastwise Shipping, in International Carriage by Sea, and in Subrogation
stem: An insurer pays the shipper in full eleven months after discharge, takes a subrogation receipt, and sues the foreign line in the twelfth month without any prior shipper notice. The line pleads prescription and want of notice. Does the suit prosper?
answer:
The suit reaches the merits, since the subrogee inherits the shipper clock and the year still runs.
Payment with assignment puts the insurer in the shipper shoes under Compañia Maritima v. Insurance Company of North America (G.R. No. L-18965, 1964), so it sues as the cargo interest rather than as a stranger.
The one-year COGSA period binds shipper with insurer alike, and filing in the twelfth month satisfies it while want of earlier notice never shortens the year.
Prescription and notice therefore both fail as bars, though the insurer must still prove the loss with the carrier fault presumption.

section: 7. Prohibited and Limiting Stipulations with Purpose, Presumption, Reduced Diligence, Fixed Recovery, Riots and Strikes, and COGSA with Its Limits
stem: A shipper signs a bill limiting recovery to invoice value for lower freight, then a strike delays the voyage for a week and the line deviates to an unscheduled port where theft guts the container. The line invokes the invoice cap and the strike clause. What survives?
answer:
Neither invocation fully survives, since deviation forfeits the cap while the strike clause covers only stoppage delay.
The signed invoice limit with lower freight satisfies Art. 1744 on its face, so it would have capped ordinary voyage loss at the declared value.
Unjustified deviation to an unscheduled port forfeits the limiting contract for the ensuing loss under Art. 1747, so the theft after deviation recovers outside the cap.
The strike clause stays valid for the week of stoppage delay under Art. 1748, yet it never reaches theft at an off-route port that carrier fault produced.

section: 7. Prohibited and Limiting Stipulations with Purpose, Presumption, Reduced Diligence, Fixed Recovery, Riots and Strikes, and COGSA with Its Limits
stem: A foreign-going bill carries no package-limit term and the shipper declares no higher value, then ten packages land short by twenty thousand dollars. The line invokes the five-hundred-dollar cap per package. Does it hold?
answer:
The cap holds and cuts recovery to five thousand dollars, since COGSA supplies the term the bill omitted.
The limitation rides in every foreign sea bill as though written there, and no higher declaration in the bill means no higher valuation binds under Sec. 4(5).
Actual loss above the cap goes unrecovered, since the section never pays beyond damage sustained and the shipper that declares low value accepts the ceiling.
The line therefore pays five hundred dollars per lost package with interest and costs as the law allows.

stem: Ysidro, a paying passenger, was on board Bus No. 904 owned and operated by Yatco Transportation Company (Yatco). He boarded the bus at Munoz, Nueva Ecija with Manila as his final destination. He was seated on the first row, window seat on the left side of the bus. As the bus was negotiating the national highway in front of the public market of Gerona, Tarlac, the bus came to a full stop because of the traffic. The driver of the bus took this opportunity to check on the tires of the bus and to relieve himself. As he was alighting from the bus to do these, an unidentified man standing along the highway hurled a huge rock at the left side of the bus and hit Ysidro between his eyes. He lost consciousness and immediately the driver, with the conductor, drove the bus to bring him to the nearest hospital. He expired before the bus could reach the hospital. Ysidro's wife and children brought a civil action to collect damages from Yatco, alleging that as a common carrier, it was required to exercise extraordinary diligence in ensuring the safety of its passengers. They contended that, in case of injuries and/or death on the part of any of its passengers, the common carrier is presumed to be at fault. In its defense, Yatco alleged that it is not an absolute insurer of its passengers and that Ysidro's death was not due to any defect in the means of transport or method of transporting passengers, or the negligent acts of its employees. Since the accident was due to the fault of a stranger over whom the common carrier had no control, or of which it did not have any prior knowledge to be able to prevent it, the cause of Ysidro's death should be considered a fortuitous event and not the liability of the common carrier. (a) Is a common carrier presumed to be at fault whenever there is death or injury to its passengers, regardless of the cause of death or injury? (2.5%) (b) What kind of diligence is required of common carriers like Yatco for the protection of its passengers? (2.5%) (c) Will your answer be the same as your answer in (b) above, if the assailant was another paying passenger who boarded the bus and deliberately stabbed Ysidro to death? (2.5%)
answer:
No to the blanket presumption, yet the diligence stays utmost and the fellow-passenger variant binds the line where prevention was possible.
The presumption of Art. 1756 runs where death or injury attends carriage, and the carrier rebuts it only with proof of the extraordinary diligence of Arts. 1733 and 1755, so a stranger act is tested by preventability rather than by insurance logic.
A rock from the roadside acquits where the crew could have done nothing with good-family care, since Art. 1763 frees the carrier for stranger harm it could not have prevented or stopped.
A stabbing by a co-passenger binds where the crew could have prevented or stopped it with the same care, since the article draws no line between strangers and fellow riders.
The heirs therefore face fair adjudication on prevention proof, with the rock case turning on the blind roadside and the knife case turning on what the conductor saw and did.

stem: A stowaway hiding in a bus toilet and a fare-paying rider beside him are both hurt when a stranger smashes a window with a bottle. The line answers the rider but disowns the stowaway. Which answers stand?
answer:
Both answers stand, since the rider holds a contract claim tested by prevention while the stowaway holds none at all.
The rider proves the ticket with the injury and the line must show utmost diligence with nothing preventable left undone under Arts. 1756 and 1763.
The stowaway proves no carriage, so no contract presumption ever arises for him and only a tort claim with fault proof could even begin.
The line therefore pays or rebuts on the rider while meeting the stowaway purely on fault if sued at all.

stem: A consignee proves the bill with short delivery of ten crates but brings no purchase invoices, then claims the highest price the goods ever fetched that year. What does the claim still lack?
answer:
The claim lacks proved value, since carriage plus shortage states liability while pesos still need proof.
The bill with the shortage engages the presumption and fixes breach, so the carrier must pay whatever loss the papers prove.
The peak price without invoices proves no pecuniary loss actually suffered, so Art. 2199 holds actual damages to adequate compensation only as duly proved.
The consignee therefore keeps liability established but recovers only the value its own evidence sustains.

stem: A line in good faith misroutes a crate of ordinary spare parts, while a second line spitefully strands a migrant worker who then loses an abroad job. How does extent differ between the two?
answer:
Extent differs by state of mind, since good faith pays the foreseeable while spite pays all reasonably attributed loss.
The misrouted parts pay the natural and probable value foreseeable at booking under the first rule of Art. 2201.
The spiteful stranding pays the lost placement with its consequences once bad faith appears under the second rule of the same article.
The worker therefore recovers wider than the parts owner though both sue in contract.

stem: A shipper claims twenty thousand dollars for ten missing crates but its own manager admits the foreign principal already reimbursed the full invoice value. The bill carries no declared higher value. What survives of the money claim?
answer:
The actual claim dies while any bad-faith correction could live on separate proof.
Reimbursement quenches pecuniary loss, so Art. 2199 leaves nothing more to compensate and British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, 1993) deletes the award.
Without a declared higher value the package limitation would have capped any surviving cargo value in any event.
The shipper therefore keeps at most moral with exemplary on fraud or bad-faith proof, never the reimbursed sum again.

section: 3. Actual/Compensatory Damages; Attorney's Fees; Interests
stem: A bus line kills a thirty-year-old father earning thirty thousand pesos a month. The heirs prove the payroll with the birth record. Walk the award from indemnity to interest.
answer:
The award stacks indemnity with capacity with interest, each on its own proof.
Death indemnity of fifty thousand pesos goes to the heirs on the death alone under the Art. 2206 package as applied in Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays (G.R. No. 186312, 2010).
Earning capacity runs two thirds of fifty years times one hundred eighty thousand pesos net yearly, which is thirty-three and one third years times one hundred eighty thousand pesos or six million pesos on full proof.
Moral follows for mental anguish under Art. 2206, exemplary follows on presumed recklessness, fees follow on a statutory door, and the total earns six percent legal interest from finality under the present rate.

stem: A line delays a bride three hours through plain mismanagement, apologizes at once, and refunds the fare in full. She sues for moral damages over ruined photographs. Does she collect?
answer: She collects no moral sum, since clean breach without fraud or bad faith draws only actual loss under Art. 2220. The refund quenches the pecuniary part and the prompt apology negates the spite that moral requires. Her ruined photographs, though genuinely painful, sound in unproved consequence rather than in Art. 2217 anguish proximately tied to a wrongful manner. The claim therefore ends with the refunded fare.

stem: A carrier pays the fifty thousand pesos death indemnity but fights the one hundred thousand pesos moral award, arguing no fraud attended the accident. The death came from its own admittedly reckless overloading. What answers the carrier?
answer: Recklessness answers the carrier, since presumed fault unrebutted in a death case is wanton enough for both moral and exemplary awards. Art. 2206 gives the spouse with descendants with ascendants moral damages for mental anguish by reason of the death alone. Presumed recklessness from unexplained overloading opens exemplary under Art. 2232 as Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays (G.R. No. 186312, 2010) holds. stem: An investor buys a light aircraft abroad and starts selling seats on weekly Boracay runs without registering the aircraft and without any Board authority. A paying guest is hurt on landing and sues on carrier liability. How does the regulatory status affect the case?
answer:
The guest still sues a common carrier because Art. 1732 turns on holding out carriage for compensation to the public and not on possession of a permit.
The lack of registration and of Board authority exposes the operator to administrative and criminal consequences and weakens every documentary defense the operator raises.
The operator therefore answers under Arts. 1755 and 1756 with presumed fault while facing the regulators separately.

stem: To celebrate her 70th birthday, A hired F Travel & Tours to arrange and facilitate her booking, ticketing, and accommodation for a two-week foreign tour, which included visits to Italy and Greece, for the total amount of PHP 145,000.00. On Wednesday, August 14, 2024, B, an employee of F Travel & Tours, went to A's house to deliver the travel documents and plane ticket. She told A to be at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) on Saturday, August 17, 2024 two hours before her flight schedule. Without checking her travel documents, A went to NAIA on Saturday, August 17, 2024. When she got there, she was informed that the flight she was supposed to take had already left the previous day. A demanded that F Travel & Tours refund her payment. She claimed that F Travel & Tours did not observe the standard of care required of a common carrier when its employee, B, informed her of the wrong flight schedule. Is F Travel & Tours liable as a common carrier? Reason(s).
answer:
F Travel & Tours is not liable as a common carrier because it only arranged booking, ticketing, and accommodation and operated no aircraft or carriage business for the public under Art. 1732.
A travel agency is an agent whose diligence is contractual agency care and not the extraordinary diligence of Arts. 1733 and 1755.
A trip on the wrong date caused by the employee's misinformation is tested under agency and fault rules with proof of actual loss and not under presumed carrier fault.
The refund therefore depends on the agency contract and on proved negligence and not on common carrier liability.

stem: To celebrate her 30th birthday party, socialite A chartered for her exclusive use the yacht usually utilized by XYZ Resort to ferry its guests from the public port to its private island. A brought her own private crew to operate the yacht and invited 30 guests to her yacht party. While in the middle of the ocean, a sudden storm caused the yacht to capsize. While all the guests survived thanks to the prompt rescue operations of XYZ Resort, A succumbed to her injuries after hitting her head on floating debris and drowning. B, A's father, sued XYZ Resorts for gross negligence, alleging that it failed to observe extraordinary diligence expected of common carriers. Is XYZ Resorts liable as a common carrier? Reason(s).
answer:
XYZ Resorts is not liable as a common carrier because A took the yacht for her exclusive use with her own private crew and full operational control, which is a demise that makes the charterer owner pro hac vice.
The resort kept no navigation or command over the capsized voyage since A supplied the crew and ran her private party on board.
The storm loss therefore cannot be laid on the resort's extraordinary diligence as carrier, and B must anchor any claim on a different source of obligation with its own proof.

stem: A foreign flag carrier flies Taipei to Manila to Cebu and offers cheap Manila to Cebu seats to fill the domestic hop. The Board stops the sale while letting the through flight continue. Is the Board correct?
answer:
The Board is correct because the Manila to Cebu leg is domestic traffic reserved by the cabotage rule even when flown as part of a foreign through service.
The fifth and higher freedoms never include the right to carry purely local passengers between two domestic points without a domestic grant.
The carrier keeps its transit and through rights but the domestic sale stays barred.

stem: A confirmed economy passenger checks in on time and the airline bumps her without asking for volunteers because the flight is overbooked. She accepts the next-day rebooking and signs a compensation receipt. May she still sue for moral damages for wounded feelings?
answer:
She may not recover beyond the receipt because compensation accepted under the overbooking rule operates as liquidated damages for the lost confirmed seat.
The carrier breached the volunteer-first rule since no passenger with a confirmed seat may be bumped without consent before volunteers are sought with rising offers.
Her signature on the compensation package therefore closes the seat-loss claim and leaves only relief outside that bargain if independently proved.

stem: A Manila to Singapore passenger checks through with one ticket and her checked bag never arrives. She declares no higher value and writes a complaint on the tenth day after arrival. The bag is still missing on the twenty-fifth day. What may she collect and is her complaint timely?
answer:
She collects up to 1,000 Special Drawing Rights under the original-treaty baggage cap since she declared no higher value and proved no intent or qualifying recklessness.
Her written complaint on the tenth day misses the seven-day baggage damage rule, so the carrier invokes the time bar unless it committed fraud.
The twenty-one-day loss rule lets her enforce the contract rights for a missing bag, but the late damage notice still defeats the claim where fraud is absent.

stem: Cargo flies Manila to Osaka and arrives water-damaged. The carrier proves the shipper packed the crate defectively and its own handlers did nothing wrong. The consignee sues on the third year after arrival. What is the outcome?
answer:
The carrier wins on the defense since defective packing by a person other than the carrier or its servants or agents exonerates it to the extent proved.
The suit also arrives dead because the two-year extinction under Art. 35 runs from arrival and the forum computation cannot revive an extinguished right.
The consignee therefore collects nothing under the Convention and domestic tort cannot reopen what exclusivity closed.

section: 1. Maritime law defined with the vessel, the Philippine flag, registry, prescription, and co-owner rights
stem: A part owner of a merchant vessel sells his undivided share to a stranger without telling the other part owners, and the sale is recorded in the mercantile registry on June 1. On June 8 the remaining part owners tender the price and claim the share. Is their claim timely and what must they still do to perfect it?
answer:
Yes, the remaining part owners acted in time and they perfect their right by delivering the price at once and anchoring their claim on the record of the sale.
Article 575 gives part owners the right of option of purchase and withdrawal in sales made to strangers, exercisable within nine days following record of the sale in the registry by delivering the price at once.
The June 8 tender falls on the seventh day from the June 1 record, so it is well within the nine-day window and the recorded sale is the exact trigger the law names.
The part owners therefore take the stranger share upon prompt delivery of the price, and the stranger buyer cannot keep what the law reserves to the ownership.

section: 2. Real and hypothecary nature with maritime lien and the limited liability rule of no vessel, no liability
stem: Absolute Timber Co. (ATC) has been engaged in the logging business in Isabela. To secure one of its shipments of logs to be transported by Andok Shipping Co., ATC purchased a marine policy with an "all risks" provision. Because of a strong typhoon then hitting Northern Luzon, the vessel sank and the shipment of logs was totally lost. ATC filed its claim, but the insurer denied the claim on several grounds, namely: (1) the vessel had not been seaworthy; (2) the vessel's crew had lacked sufficient training; (3) the improper loading of the logs on only one side of the vessel had led to the tilting of the ship to that side during the stormy voyage; and (4) the extremely bad weather had been a fortuitous event. ATC now seeks your legal advice to know if its claim was sustainable. What is your advice? Explain your answer. (3%)
answer:
I advise ATC that its claim is sustainable and that the four grounds for denial all fail against the carrier negligence shown.
A common carrier must observe extraordinary diligence and a typhoon that regularly visits Northern Luzon is an ordinary vicissitude of the voyage rather than a fortuitous event once unseaworthiness, an untrained crew, and one-sided loading concurred to sink the vessel.
The unseaworthy condition at sailing, the lack of crew training, and the improper stowage point to concurrent fault of the shipowner, so the defense of force majeure collapses and the limited liability rule of no vessel and no liability cannot shelter the owner under the doctrine of *Phil-Am General Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals* (G.R. No. 116940, 1997).
ATC therefore recovers on the all-risks policy and the insurer as subrogee takes the same action against Andok Shipping, because the proximate cause of the total loss was carrier fault and not the weather alone.

section: 3. Protests with admiralty jurisdiction, smuggling forfeiture, and marine pollution
stem: The captain limps into a strange Philippine port with a sprung mast and no ship agent in sight, fearing seizure by privateers reported along his course. What must he file within twenty-four hours and before whom, and what paper proves he complied?
answer:
The captain must present himself to the maritime authority within twenty-four hours and file a sworn declaration of the vessel name, registry, port of departure, cargo, and cause of arrival.
Article 612 makes this protest an inherent duty of the captain whenever he makes a port in distress, and the authority vises the declaration when found acceptable.
The vised certificate proving arrival in distress and its reasons is the paper that proves compliance, and it anchors the later ruling on whether the arrival was proper or improper.
Without that timely protest the shipowner loses the evidentiary root of a proper arrival and stays exposed to the cargo claims the voyage break caused.

stem: A foreign vessel on a Singapore to Manila run loads Manila to Cebu boxes between foreign legs and files no transshipment manifest. May it carry them?
answer:
No because the Manila to Cebu leg is domestic cargo reserved to Philippine bottoms under R.A. No. 9295.
R.A. No. 10668 allows a foreign vessel to co-load only foreign cargo for transshipment and never domestic cargo under Secs. 4 and 8.
The operator without a manifest and without a Marina special permit therefore has no paper for the domestic lift.
The boxes must move on a Philippine vessel while the foreign vessel keeps only its foreign cargo.

section: 5. Persons in maritime commerce with ship agents, captains, and officers
stem: A ship agent without owner authority orders the vessel on a new voyage and insures her with an unsound underwriter. The venture fails. Who bears the loss?
answer:
The agent bears it because a new voyage with new insurance needs owner or majority authority under Art. 598.
Acts inside repairs, equipment, and navigation needs bind ownership, but unauthorized new voyages and charters stay personal to the agent.
The insurer insolvency therefore falls subsidiarily on the agent who insured without authority.
The owner answers only for authorized navigation needs proved to benefit the vessel.

section: 6. Special contracts with charter parties, bills of lading, and bottomry and respondentia
stem: Onassis Shipping, Inc. (Onassis) operated passenger vessels and cargo trucks, and offered its services to the general public. In line with its vision and mission to protect the environment, Go-Green Asia (Go-Green), an NGO affiliated with Greenpeace, entered into a contract with Onassis whereby Go-Green would operate with its own crew the MN Dolphin, an ocean-going passenger vessel of Onassis. While on its way to Palawan carrying Go-Green's invited guests who were international and local observers desirous of checking certain environmental concerns in the area, the MN Dolphin encountered high waves and strong winds caused by a typhoon in the West Philippine Sea. The rough seas led to serious physical injuries to some of the guests. Discuss the liabilities of Onassis and Go-Green to the passengers of the M/V Dolphin. Explain briefly your answer. (3%)
answer:
Go-Green answers as owner pro hac vice because it ran the vessel with its own crew and full command, which is a demise shifting carrier character to the charterer under Planters Products (G.R. No. 101503, 1993).
Onassis kept bare ownership but ran no navigation on that voyage, so it does not answer as carrier for the onboard injuries.
Go-Green must therefore meet carrier diligence for its guests and rebut presumed fault with seaworthiness and storm unavoidability.
Onassis pays nothing absent its own fault since control decides everything in charter liability.

section: 6. Special contracts with charter parties, bills of lading, and bottomry and respondentia
stem: The master faces an imminent storm and deliberately jettisons hold bales to save ship and remaining cargo, then brings the venture safely to port. The shippers of the saved bales refuse to contribute, arguing that only the shipowner should pay for saving his own vessel. Who contributes and on what basis?
answer:
All saved interests contribute, and the objecting shippers pay their proportionate share of the jettison.
The jettison was a deliberate sacrifice against a real and known common peril threatening vessel and cargo together, which is the textbook definition of general average under Article 811.
Article 812 makes every person with an interest in vessel and cargo at the time contribute, with the vessel, the saved cargo, and half the freight forming the contributing capital.
The saved shippers therefore share the indemnity of the jettisoned bales pro rata, because general average spreads a sacrifice made for all upon all whom it saved.

section: 8. Ship Mortgage Decree 1978 (preferred mortgage meaning/requirements, preferred claims, executory contract doctrine, prescription/laches, necessaries liens, maritime tort, salvage lien, subrogation, mortgage with other properties, arrest/foreclosure)
stem: A bank records a whole-vessel mortgage with the good-faith affidavit and keeps its preference. On foreclosure the proceeds cannot pay everyone. Name in exact order the seven grades that beat the bank mortgage.
answer:
The seven grades that beat the foreclosing mortgage run courts and taxes, crew, average, salvage, prior liens, tort, and prior mortgages.
Section 17 of Presidential Decree No. 1521 gives the preferred mortgage priority over all claims except the following in the order stated, namely court costs and taxes, crew wages, general average, salvage with contract salvage, maritime liens prior in time to recordation, tort damages, and earlier recorded preferred mortgages.
The bank mortgage therefore pays only after every one of these grades is satisfied in full, with claimants inside the same grade sharing pro rata when proceeds fall short.
This fixed ladder is why a mortgagee searches the record and demands disclosure of prior liens before parting with the loan.

section: 9. Salvage Law (kinds, compensation, limit, excluded persons, jetsam/flotsam, rights/obligations)
stem: A fishing crew spots a burning yacht abandoned by its panic-stricken owner, and a passing tug that owes the yacht nothing tows her to port while the crew helps lash the line. Both claim salvage. Who earns and who is excluded?
answer:
The passing tug earns the reward and the fishing crew shares only if its help went beyond crew duty and the tug accepts it.
Section 8 denies reward to the crew of the vessel in danger, while a stranger who voluntarily conveys abandoned sea property to safety with success earns under Section 1.
The tug as pure salvor takes a court-measured reward up to the fifty percent limit secured by a fourth-grade salvage lien, and the crew members who merely did their duty take nothing.
Only voluntary extra help accepted by the salvor can share in the award, because salvage pays successful strangers and never the hands already bound to the imperiled vessel.

section: 1. Public Utility Concept; Public Service under PSA
stem: A company owns no power plant and merely advances the building-wide Meralco bill while collecting each tenant's metered share. The tenants complain to the regulator that the company sells electricity without a franchise. Is the company a public service subject to regulation.
answer: No, because the three-element Sec. 13(b) test fails on ownership or control of a covered service. The law requires ownership, operation, management, or control of an enterprise supplying electric light, heat, and power for hire or compensation as a business, and a mere administrator who advances and recovers billings owns and controls no plant while the utility supplies the tenants directly. The ruling in Cruz de Syquia (G.R. Nos. L-42783-85, 1976) annulled the same kind of board orders and left the pro-rata dispute to the regular courts as a civil lease question.

stem: A bus operator with existing certificates applies for additional units and the regulator adds a twenty-five-year expiry to all its certificates without any hearing. The operator assails the whole statute as undue delegation. How should the challenge fail and the order fall.

stem: TRUE or FALSE. Explain briefly your answer. (b) The term capital in relation to public utilities under Sec. 11, Art. XII of the 1987 Constitution refers to the total outstanding capital stock comprising both common and non-voting preferred shares. (2%)
answer: FALSE, because capital in Sec. 11 Art. XII means only shares entitled to vote in the election of directors and never the total outstanding stock with non-voting preferred shares. The law ties control to electing directors and demands full beneficial ownership with voting rights, so the sixty-forty test applies to voting shares under the 2011 decision in Gamboa (G.R. A corporation whose foreigners hold the voting common shares fails the test even when Filipinos hold all the non-voting preferred shares.

section: 3. Constitutional Provisions and Limitations
stem: A water district charter provides that no other franchise for water service inside the district may issue without board consent. A cooperative seeks a franchise and the board refuses. Is the consent requirement valid.
answer: No, because the Constitution bans every exclusive franchise whether created directly or indirectly. The law states that no franchise, certificate, or authorization for a public utility shall be exclusive in character, and police power includes no power to violate that ban. The book rule voids Sec. 47 of P.D. No. 198 as amended for creating exclusivity through a consent veto, following the RCPI mandate (G.R. No. L-68729, 1987) that one operator never blocks another.

Yes. The governing broadcast law makes the congressional franchise a condition sine qua non, and later laws vesting certificate powers in the NTC never repealed that exaction. stem: A certificate holder disobeys voltage and metering directives for eight straight years, cures nothing after inspection reports and hearings, and pleads that the Commission must impose only the daily fine. Must the Commission settle for a fine.
answer:
No, because willful and contumacious refusal to obey orders and certificate conditions warrants revocation and the fine remedy is only cumulative and additional.
The law empowers the Commission to suspend or revoke where the holder violated or willfully and contumaciously refused to obey any order, rule, regulation, or provision of law, and the last sentence of Sec. 21 keeps every other remedy intact so a fine never blocks cancellation.
The ruling in Rizal Light v. Morong (G.R. Nos. L-20993 and L-21221, 1968) sustained revocation on exactly such an eight-year record of neglect since protection of investment shields only operators of good standing.
The Commission therefore revokes the certificate and forfeits the franchise on substantial evidence instead of stopping at a fine.

section: 1. Due Process: Alternative Penalty, NTC Against Legislative Franchise, Hearing Rule
stem: The NTC cancels the CPC of a broadcast station that operates under a congressional franchise, and the station invokes free speech and prior restraint. May the NTC end the franchise by cancelling the certificate.
answer:
No, because the NTC has no power to cancel the legislative franchise behind the certificate and cancellation of the operating license operates as a death sentence on broadcast speech.
The Constitution protects broadcast media under the free-speech, expression, and press guarantees even while scarcity justifies regulation, and the franchise-plus-certificate framework already imposes fees, fines, and mandates through valid rule-making without ending the grant.
The ruling in Albano v. Reyes (G.R. No. 83551, 1989) confirms that franchise authority and agency authorization are distinct layers since a delegated contract with presidential approval can authorize operation where Congress supplied the delegation.
The NTC therefore keeps its fining and rule-making powers but leaves repeal of the franchise to Congress when the common good so requires.

stem: The Commission suspended a certificate without prior hearing, the operator moved for reconsideration raising every merit and defense it would have raised at the original hearing, and the Commission granted partial relief after full argument. Was due process denied.
answer:
No, because the later full hearing on reconsideration cured the earlier want of prior notice and hearing.
The law requires notice and hearing before suspension or revocation, yet the defect is procedural and curable where the operator actually adduced evidence, faced the record, and argued through counsel on reconsideration.
The ruling in Rizal Light v. Morong (G.R. Nos. L-20993 and L-21221, 1968) treats hearing objections as waived unless timely raised and cures process through the granted reconsideration.
The suspension therefore stands as a valid exercise of the Sec. 16(n) power with the thirty-day pre-hearing limit observed.

section: 2. Rate Regulation: Police Power, Non-Delegation, Deregulation, Just Standard, Expenses, Provisional Increase, Collection
stem: The LTFRB authorizes provincial bus operators to collect the P0.37 per kilometer fare plus a floating band of fifteen percent over it at their own discretion, and a later increase compounds on the collected figure. Commuters challenge the band as surrender of rate power. Is the band valid.
answer:
No, because the band lets each operator fix its own effective fare and amounts to an undue delegation of the delegated rate power.
The law delegates rate fixing to the regulator under the fair and reasonable standard, the operator may propose new rates but never makes them effective without prior approval on evidence, and the regulator cannot decide in advance that unknown future rates are just.
The ruling in Pangasinan Transportation v. PSC (G.R. No. 47065, 1940) roots rate control in police power that the agency must actually exercise instead of surrendering to carriers.
The band therefore falls as illegal and invalid while the base authorized fare survives until lawfully changed.

section: 2. Rate Regulation: Police Power, Non-Delegation, Deregulation, Just Standard, Expenses, Provisional Increase, Collection
stem: The regulator approves a provisional rate increase without hearing on urgent public need, publishes notice to affected parties, and opens the ratification hearing on the fifteenth day. The utility collects the provisional rate meanwhile. Was the procedure lawful.
answer:
Yes, because provisional rates are temporary and adjustable and the law expressly allows approval without necessity of any hearing with a hearing within fifteen days after.
The grant must publish notice to the affected territory, must convene the hearing to ratify, change, modify, or alter the provisional figure on public interest, and must fold the provisional collections into the definitive rate after final hearing.
The ruling in PLDT v. NTC (G.R. No. 88404, 1990) treats provisional relief as limited, non-exclusive, and revocable with the merits reserved for the main case.
The collections therefore stand pending the hearing outcome with refund or adjustment to follow the final rate.

stem: An electric utility books its income tax payments as operating expenses, asks a return on that item, and defends the entry as a cost of doing business. Consumers oppose the pass-through. Must the regulator allow the item.
answer:
No, because income tax never forms part of operating expenses and its burden stays with the taxpayer alone.
Operating expenses must be reasonable, recurring, and attributable to production of the service so the utility recoups prudent costs and earns a return above them, while income tax is an excise on the privilege of earning that benefits no customer and yields no service revenue.
The return cases from Republic v. Meralco (G.R. Nos. 141314 and 141369, 2002) fix the fair-return-on-property standard with expenses limited to service-related prudent costs.
The regulator therefore disallows the item and sets the rate without shifting the tax to consumers.

stem: A utility sells ten percent of its stock to an alien and Filipino holdings fall to fifty-five percent of capital. The parties call the sale private and internal. What follows for the sale and the certificate.
answer:
The sale is void and of no effect and independently supplies cause to cancel the certificate.
The law voids every alien transfer that in itself or with connected previous sales drops Philippine citizens below sixty per centum, and the same transfer expressly warrants cancellation of the authority to operate.
The constitutional sixty percent Filipino ownership rule in Art. XII Sec. 11 anchors the statutory floor construed in Gamboa v. Teves (G.R. No. 176579, 2011) with full beneficial ownership.
The Commission therefore strikes the transfer from the books and opens cancellation while the parties renegotiate a compliant Filipino-majority structure.

stem: The NTC fines a broadcast station P100,000 per day for operating after its provisional authority lapsed, without any prior notice or hearing, and the station claims the fine needs a criminal case in court. Is the fine valid.
answer:
The fine as imposed is void, though the NTC holds the fining power and no criminal case is needed.
The law empowers the successor agency to fine for violation of certificate terms after due notice and hearing within the P5,000 to P2,000,000 daily range, and such proceedings are administrative and regulatory rather than penal with prescription under Act No. 3326 instead of court rules.
Temporary permits never bar fines for post-expiry operation, yet notice and hearing remain indispensable to the quasi-judicial act.
The NTC therefore re-issues the fine only after proper notice and hearing, with refund, suspension until payment, and court enforcement available as cumulative remedies.

section: 1. Competition and Importance; Constitutional Provisions; Policies and Rationale
stem: Congress deregulates the cement industry but keeps a prior-import-volume rule that only the two incumbent importers can meet, and no newcomer can sell a bag without five years of import records. A newcomer assails the rule as an entry barrier. Will the challenge prosper.
answer:
Yes, because the rule entrenches the incumbents and shuts newcomers out of a supposedly open market.
Section 19 of Article XII commands the State to regulate or prohibit monopolies as public interest requires and absolutely bans combinations in restraint of trade with unfair competition.
The ruling in Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, 1997) struck down a deregulation law whose tariff, inventory, and pricing rules built walls only the oligopoly could climb.
The prior-volume rule therefore falls as an unconstitutional barrier to a truly competitive market.

section: 1. Competition and Importance; Constitutional Provisions; Policies and Rationale
stem: A mayor claims that the Constitution bans every monopoly so the city may seize the only ice plant in town without regulation. The owner answers that the plant charges fair prices and serves all buyers. May the city skip regulation and proceed to seizure.
answer:
No, because the Constitution bans no monopoly per se and commands regulation or prohibition only when the public interest so requires.
A lone plant that serves all buyers at fair prices holds a factual monopoly without a prohibited combination, so the State must first test the facts against the public interest standard.
The ruling in Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, 1997) treats Section 19 as an anti-trust command against entry barriers and not as an automatic death sentence on every large firm, a reading confirmed in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, 2019).
The city therefore regulates before it prohibits and seizes nothing without law and just compensation.

section: 2. Methods to Deter Anti-competitive Conduct; Tools under the PCA
stem: All four refiners agree to fix pump prices and rotate winning bids for government fuel. The finance manager who signed the minutes seeks immunity and tells everything after the inquiry has started. The Department of Justice charges the presidents. Who goes to jail and what happens to the manager.
answer:
The knowing and willful presidents face two to seven years with a P50,000,000 to P250,000,000 fine each while the manager may earn leniency but never automatic immunity.
Section 30 punishes every Section 14(a) and 14(b) agreement per violation on responsible officers, and price fixing with bid rotation sits per se prohibited so no efficiency defense saves it.
Section 35 grants a late reporter leniency only as the first to come forward with full and continuing cooperation where conviction evidence is still lacking and fairness allows.
The presidents therefore stand trial for the cartel while the manager keeps only a chance at leniency.

section: 2. Methods to Deter Anti-competitive Conduct; Tools under the PCA
stem: A consumer group proves a flour mill abused its dominant position and asks the Commission for P80,000,000 on first offense plus damages for every baker overcharged. The mill argues one forum must choose one remedy. Must the Commission stop at the fine.
answer:
No, because the administrative fine and the private civil action answer different injuries and run on separate tracks.
Section 29 lets the Commission fine up to P100,000,000 on first offense after notice and hearing with gravity and duration guiding the amount, and Section 45 lets every directly injured person sue separately after the preliminary inquiry closes.
The mill pays the State for the violation and pays the bakers for their losses, with triple fines if flour counts as a basic necessity.
The Commission therefore imposes the fine while the bakers pursue their own civil case.

section: 3. Scope of the PCA; Relevant Market Rule; Single Economic Unit Rule
stem: Two shipping lines serve the same island route and charge identical fares. A new entrant proves passengers treat the two lines as fully swappable but proves freight from the rival port costs twice as much with twice the sailing time. The lines claim one national market while the entrant claims an island market. Which market controls.
answer:
The island market controls if competition conditions there stay homogenous and differ from the national picture.
The relevant geographic market turns on where supply and demand truly meet with shared conditions, and Section 24 weighs distribution cost with time to supply and the cost and probability of users seeking other ports.
Passenger swappability fixes the product market while island freight and sailing time split the geography.
The Commission therefore defines the island as the relevant geographic market before testing dominance and abuse inside it.

section: 3. Scope of the PCA; Relevant Market Rule; Single Economic Unit Rule
stem: 3. Ernest Bicycle Corporation (EBC) and Max Speed Corporation (MSC) are the leading manufacturers and sellers of electric bicycles in the country. EBC and MSC offer their bestselling models at PHP 25,000.00 per unit. In 2023, Gryffin Pedals, Inc. (GPI) entered the market and sold electric bicycles with features similar to EBC and MSC's bestselling models for only PHP 20,000.00. GPI has no physical stores and offers its products in digital marketplaces. After a year, GPI had 75% share of the market leaving EBC and MSC at 15% and 10% shares, respectively. EBC and MSC filed a complaint before the Philippine Competition Commission and alleged that GPI is fast monopolizing the electric bicycles market because of its dominant position. Will the complaint against GPI for violation of the competition laws prosper? Explain.
answer:
No, because a seventy-five percent share only presumes a dominant position while the Act punishes abuse of that position and never the position itself.
Section 27 raises a rebuttable presumption of dominance at fifty percent share yet shields share gained through superior skill, service, product, and business acumen, and Section 15 condemns only conduct that substantially prevents, restricts, or lessens competition such as below-cost selling with the object of destroying rivals.
GPI sells a similar bicycle twenty percent cheaper through an efficient no-store marketplace model, and nothing shows selling below cost to kill rivals, entry barriers, or exclusionary conditions rather than legitimate price rivalry that benefits consumers.
The complaint therefore fails on dominance alone while EBC and MSC must still prove abusive conduct inside a properly defined relevant market.

section: 1. Anti-competitive Agreements
stem: All four refiners agree in a group chat to fix pump prices and rotate winning bids for municipal fuel. The finance manager who typed the minutes claims the deal was oral and informal so no agreement exists. Is the cartel per se prohibited.
answer:
Yes, because price fixing with bid rotation among competitors is condemned per se with no weighing of harm against efficiency.
Section 14(a) punishes restricting competition as to price and fixing price in any bidding with cover bidding, suppression, rotation, allocation, and analogous manipulation, while agreement covers every tacit, oral, and informal concerted action.
The ruling in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, 2019) still requires the Commission to define the market and weigh effects for other agreements, but per se cartels need no such weighing.
The chat therefore proves the agreement and the managers face prosecution with the entity fined.

section: 1. Anti-competitive Agreements
stem: Two cement makers divide towns by buyer with one taking north distributors and the other taking south distributors. A new entrant proves the division, and the makers answer that no price was ever fixed. Must the Commission still weigh effects before condemning the pact.
answer:
Yes, because market division by buyers answers under Section 14(b) only where object or effect substantially lessens competition.
Section 14(b)(2) prohibits dividing or sharing the market by volume, territory, goods, buyers, sellers, or any other means with that substantial-harm test, and Section 26 requires market definition with harm weighed against efficiency gains.
The ruling in Eastern Telecommunications v. ICC (G.R. No. 135992, 2004) favors open rivalry over carved-up territories, since no operator holds a vested right to a fenced market.
The Commission therefore defines the cement market, tests substantial harm against any proven efficiency, and condemns the pact where harm prevails.

section: 2. Abuse of Dominant Position
stem: A dominant flour mill sells below cost for six months with internal memos targeting the death of a new rival mill. A second dominant mill only matches the first mill price in good faith for comparable flour. Which mill abuses its position.
answer:
The first mill abuses while the second stays lawful, because object separates predation from competition.
Section 15(a) condemns below-cost selling with the object of driving competition out of the relevant market yet expressly saves prices set in good faith to meet a rival price for the same or comparable product of like quality.
The memos prove destructive object for the first mill while good-faith matching shields the second, and dominance alone condemns neither without abusive conduct.
The Commission therefore pursues the predator and clears the matcher.

section: 2. Abuse of Dominant Position
stem: A dominant bottler charges provincial dealers a higher price than Manila dealers for identical drinks on identical terms, and the gap tracks no cost, volume, or rival-price difference. The bottler answers that price gaps are normal business. Is the differential permissible.
answer:
No, because unreasonable discrimination among contemporaneous traders on similar terms abuses where competition substantially lessens.
Section 15(d) condemns such gaps while saving only four differentials, namely socialized pricing for the less fortunate, cost-reflecting differences, responses to rival prices or facilities, and changes driven by market conditions, marketability, or volume.
No saving clause fits a gap that tracks no cost, volume, or rivalry, and the effect on provincial dealers is exclusion from fair rivalry.
The differential therefore falls outside every permissible class and answers as abuse.

section: 3. Mergers and Acquisitions Control
stem: Two beverage giants breach both operative thresholds and sign on June 1 with notice filed the same day. They close on June 11 before any decision. The giants claim the ten-day sprint harmed no one. What is the status of the closing.
answer:
The closing is void and both giants face an administrative fine of one percent to five percent of the transaction value.
Section 17 bars consummation until thirty days after notification and voids any agreement closed in breach, with the fine keyed to transaction value rather than to proven harm.
The ten-day sprint therefore jumps the gun even if the market felt nothing yet, and the Commission may still review the deal on the merits.
The parties must re-notify and wait out the clock with penalties paid.

section: 3. Mergers and Acquisitions Control
stem: A buyer takes control of a rival in four monthly slices within one year, with each slice below threshold but all four combined above it. The buyer files nothing and claims each slice stands alone. Must the buyer have notified.
answer:
Yes, because successive acquisitions within one year between the same parties count as one transaction for notification.
The creeping-transaction rule treats slices and part-acquisitions inside the one-year window as a single deal, reckoned from the binding preliminary agreement where one exists and otherwise from the last step that pushes the total past the thresholds.
The buyer therefore owed notice once the combined slices breached both tests, and closing the last slice without notice voids it with a one to five percent fine.
Splitting one takeover into small steps never defeats compulsory notification.

section: 1. Philippine Competition Commission
stem: The Secretary of Energy writes the Commission directing it to clear a refinery merger without review because the project is a presidential priority. The merging refiners invoke the letter and demand immediate clearance. Must the Commission obey the directive.
answer:
No, because the Commission is an independent quasi-judicial body that decides only on evidence after due process.
Section 5 creates the Commission as independent although attached to the Office of the President for administration, while Section 12 gives it original and primary jurisdiction over merger review and Section 31 gives it sole and exclusive authority to open and close inquiries.
A cabinet letter is neither evidence nor law, and the ruling in Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, 1997) struck down executive implementation that rewrote congressional competition standards.
The Commission therefore disregards the directive and runs the notification and review clock on the merits.

section: 1. Philippine Competition Commission
stem: After due hearing the Commission finds a cement cartel and orders the members to sell two plants although a supervised price and supply commitment would restore rivalry. The cartel answers that divestiture is a listed remedy so the Commission may choose it freely. Is the divestiture order valid.
answer:
No, because structural remedies issue only where behavioral relief cannot do the job.
Section 12(h) allows adjustment and divestiture orders only where no equally effective behavioral remedy exists or where the behavioral option would burden the enterprise more, and only in proportion to a lasting or repeated infringement risk rooted in the structure itself.
The finding here admits that a supervised commitment would restore rivalry, so the first condition fails and the order punishes structure instead of curing conduct.
The Commission must replace divestiture with the effective behavioral remedy and reserve structural surgery for a case that proves its necessity.

section: 2. Composition, Term, Qualification; Confidentiality; Remedies of the Entity
stem: A business daily demands that the Commission publish the production costs and customer lists a cement maker filed during a cartel inquiry. The maker objects and withholds consent while no court orders disclosure. Must the Commission publish the data.
answer:
No, because confidential business information filed in an inquiry shall never be disclosed without consent or a lawful disclosure order.
Section 34 seals operations, production, sales, shipments, customer identities, inventories, and income data against direct or indirect disclosure, publication, transfer, copying, or dissemination, and breach draws a fine of not less than P1,000,000.00 but not more than P5,000,000.00.
Consent is absent here and no law or valid court or regulatory order compels release, so none of the three exceptions opens.
The Commission therefore keeps the data sealed and publishes only a ruling redacted to the extent possible.

section: 2. Composition, Term, Qualification; Confidentiality; Remedies of the Entity
stem: A flour distributor directly injured by a price cartel files a civil damages suit in the Regional Trial Court while the Commission preliminary inquiry is still running. The cartel moves to dismiss as premature. Must the court dismiss the suit.
answer:
Yes, because a private action opens only after the Commission completes its preliminary inquiry.
Section 45 lets any person who suffers direct injury sue separately and independently only after completion of the Section 31 preliminary inquiry, and Section 31 gives the Commission sole and exclusive authority to open that inquiry with a ninety-day completion rule.
The ruling in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, 2019) dismisses competition claims pleaded without the ultimate facts that an inquiry first builds, so a suit filed mid-inquiry jumps the administrative gate.
The court therefore dismisses the suit as premature without prejudice to refiling once the Commission completes its inquiry.
